# Metric Learning for Few-Shot Image Classification: An Embedding–Representation–Metric Comparison

## Abstract

Metric-learning few-shot classifiers are best compared by where their main bias acts: the encoder, the support-set class model, or the comparison rule. Embedding losses and modulation target transferable features; nearest examples, prototypes, distributions and subspaces encode support information differently; fixed, learned, query-conditioned and task-adaptive comparators vary decision flexibility. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:0fa86bc29e24] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:0b0752f4ac3d] [E:arxiv:2006.11325:abstract:claim:d76dc15743ab] Reported gains do not support one universal winner. K-tuplet and Proto-Triplet/ICNN show embedding and cross-dataset benefits, distribution and subspace methods address uncertainty or geometry, and RCN or MACO add learned relational comparison, but results differ in backbone, shots, datasets, pretraining, inference and label budget. In-domain, cross-domain, sensor-domain and label-efficient transfer settings must therefore be compared separately. ## Introduction

Few-shot image classification asks a model to assign query images to classes when each novel class supplies only a small labeled support set, commonly one to five examples. The central difficulty is that ordinary supervised training can overfit to these few labels; metric-learning approaches respond by learning an embedding space and/or a similarity function in which same-class samples are close and different-class samples are far apart, then classifying a query by its relation to support samples or aggregated class representations. This review therefore compares approaches by the stage at which their main inductive bias operates: the image embedding, the class representation, and the distance or comparison rule. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:0fa86bc29e24] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1]

The standard episode makes the comparison structure explicit: a support set contains the few labeled images for the task's classes, and a query set contains unlabeled images from those classes. A feature encoder maps both sets into an embedding space, after which a metric function compares query features with support examples or class models to produce predictions. This framing covers nearest-example methods, prototype methods, distribution or subspace models, and learned relation networks, while excluding methods whose main mechanism is gradient-based task adaptation rather than comparison in a learned space. [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:aafe927bcc74] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:efa61445b15c]

The organizing choice used here is the review's three-stage grouping—learning feature embeddings, learning class representations, and learning distance measures—rather than a universal taxonomy. These dimensions are complementary: one method may improve the encoder, another may replace a mean prototype with a distribution or subspace, and a third may replace a fixed Euclidean or cosine comparison with a learned relation model. Metric learning can also be trained episodically as meta-learning, so the labels “metric-based” and “meta-learning” are not mutually exclusive. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb]

The comparison must also distinguish in-domain from cross-domain evaluation. In the familiar mini-ImageNet-style protocol, base and novel classes are drawn from the same benchmark domain; in cross-domain few-shot learning, the model is trained on one source domain, such as mini-ImageNet, and tested on novel classes from datasets such as CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, Stanford Cars, or Caltech-101. Consequently, accuracy under same-domain episodes does not by itself establish robustness to domain shift, and later sections keep datasets, shots, backbones, baselines, and training settings together before drawing any comparative conclusion. [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:aafe927bcc74] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:53d7fbe2de7c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:22bea6df5855]

## Background and Method Taxonomy

Taxonomy used in this review. The methods are organized by the three metric-learning stages identified in the reviewed survey: learning feature embeddings, learning class representations, and learning distance or similarity measures. This is an analytical grouping for comparing mechanisms, not a claim that every paper uses these labels or that a model belongs to only one stage. A single architecture can contribute at several stages—for example, an episodic encoder, an aggregated prototype, and a learned relation module can be trained end to end. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb]

Embedding-centered approaches place most of the model's adaptation burden on the feature map. Their premise is that a discriminative, task-general embedding should pull same-class images together and push different-class images apart before the final comparison. Examples in the sources include Siamese-style and triplet-like embedding learning, deep K-tuplet learning with multiple negatives, task-specific feature transformers or modulation, self-attention or multi-stage embeddings, and query–support Transformers that refine representations using context from the whole episode. These methods still need a decision rule, but their main novelty is what counts as a comparable feature and whether features are task-agnostic or task-conditioned. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_few_shot_deep_metric_learning_methods:0:c53378070ee7:claim:f4690eeeb5d0] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:abe1e207bc9c] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:2:ada74c4d4774:claim:83310823f8ec] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:baa36cba9b0a] [E:arxiv:2208.12398:abstract:claim:eb85178b6852]

Class-representation approaches differ in how the few support examples summarize a class. Early nearest-example methods compare a query directly with individual support embeddings. Point-prototype methods replace that set of comparisons with a reference vector, typically a simple or weighted mean of support features. Distributional and subspace approaches instead model uncertainty or geometric structure: variational representations estimate class distributions and can use KL divergence, Deep Subspace Network represents each class by a low-dimensional subspace and assigns a query by nearest projected distance, while SRL represents images or class templates as subspaces in local CNN feature space. The relevant distinction is therefore not merely “prototype versus non-prototype,” but whether a class is encoded as isolated points, one vector, a distribution, or a subspace. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:32d2f0aedf14] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8969ee1e4e70]

Distance-centered approaches vary the comparison rule after features and class summaries are formed. Fixed-rule methods use a predefined relation such as Euclidean or cosine distance. Learned-similarity methods train a network to score query–support or query–prototype pairs; Relation Network and Region Comparison Network fall in this broad family, with RCN additionally designed to expose corresponding image regions through its comparison and visualization mechanism. A further distinction is that a learned comparator producing class scores is not necessarily a mathematical metric: MACO explicitly replaces metric-space comparison with a neural classifier and conditions class representations on the query, so its authors describe it as metric-agnostic rather than a true metric-learning method. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:efa61445b15c] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:0fa86bc29e24] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:8ddae53d33c7] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:2:c37dc575d3c8:claim:d5aad7ce0ffb] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:1:74ed040863a6:claim:3812293ab161]

Task conditioning supplies another useful comparison axis. A task-invariant metric assumes one embedding and comparison rule can transfer across episodes from a similar domain, whereas task-specific methods adapt features, metrics, or class representations to the current support set. The Meta-Metric-Learner paper motivates this split by arguing that a single task-invariant metric is strained when tasks contain varying class counts or come from less similar domains; it combines a task-specific metric learner with a meta-learner that specifies the base model. Likewise, cross-domain feature-wise modulation targets distribution shift by perturbing encoder activations during training so the downstream metric is less tied to seen-domain feature statistics. These axes cut across the three-stage taxonomy: conditioning may be implemented in the encoder, class model, comparator, or a hybrid meta-model. [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:0b0752f4ac3d] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:d539e10e3cd6] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:2:ada74c4d4774:claim:83310823f8ec] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:aafe927bcc74]

Boundaries and adjacent objectives. Metric-based few-shot classification should be distinguished from optimization-based meta-learning, whose central mechanism is learning an initialization or update rule for task-specific parameters, and from ordinary transfer learning or fine-tuning, where a source-pretrained classifier is adapted to target labels. These paradigms can overlap: metric embeddings may be learned through episodic meta-training, and self-supervised or transfer-trained embeddings may later be used with prototypes. The taxonomy also should not be confused with zero-shot recognition, which compares images to semantic class descriptions or attributes rather than to a few labeled support images, or with domain-specific applications such as SAR and hyperspectral classification, where metric learning is a method rather than a separate task definition. Efficiency, interpretability, and cross-domain robustness are evaluation objectives or design constraints; they do not by themselves define a separate metric-learning family. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:efa61445b15c] [E:arxiv:2006.11325:abstract:claim:d76dc15743ab] [E:arxiv:1607.08085:abstract:claim:062328880b00] [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:616f72ed5776] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:430d78b68501]

## Representative Methods

Embedding-first metric learners treat the encoder as the main learned component while keeping the final comparison relatively simple. Their common mechanism is to optimize a deep embedding so that images from the same class are mapped nearby and images from different classes are separated, then classify novel queries by nearest support examples, prototypes, or another distance-based rule. This family is appropriate when the central concern is transfer of visual features to unseen classes, but it does not remove the need to specify how support examples are aggregated or how distance is computed. The reviewed survey places embedding learning as the first of its three metric-learning stages and lists task-agnostic features, task-specific features, augmentation, multi-task learning, and semi-supervised variants within that broad stage. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_few_shot_deep_metric_learning_methods:0:c53378070ee7:claim:f4690eeeb5d0] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb] Deep K-tuplet Network makes the embedding objective more episode-like than an ordinary triplet loss. A standard triplet update compares an anchor with one positive and one negative, whereas few-shot episodes require a query to be discriminated from several competing classes; the K-tuplet formulation jointly compares against K negative samples in each mini-batch and uses semi-hard mining to select informative triplets, speed convergence, and stabilize training. Its authors present the method as a strong feature-embedding baseline and state that the learned embedding can be combined with a learnable non-linear distance metric. The evidence they claim is competitive mini-ImageNet performance relative to metric-based and other meta-based methods and stronger cross-dataset transfer when training on mini-ImageNet and testing on Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, and Stanford Cars. Its applicability boundary is that the reported cross-domain result concerns a model trained on mini-ImageNet and evaluated on those specific target datasets; it should not be generalized to arbitrary domain shifts without matched evaluation. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:abe1e207bc9c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:53d7fbe2de7c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:22bea6df5855] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:307bf74255b7] Proto-Triplet and the ICNN loss are later embedding-loss methods that explicitly constrain latent-space geometry rather than only optimizing episodic classification. Proto-Triplet adapts triplet-style optimization to the few-shot setting, while ICNN uses an inter-class and intra-class nearest-neighbor score to assess and improve embedding separability. The paper reports that these losses improved mini-ImageNet accuracy by about 2 percentage points over compared metric-based few-shot methods and also showed competitive generalization on Caltech, CUB, Dogs, and Cars. Because the available source states aggregate claims rather than the full backbone, shot-by-shot results, and training recipe, the supported conclusion is that the losses target embedding compactness and separation; a precise ranking against methods with different architectures or protocols is not warranted from this evidence alone. [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:2b40d78bb79f] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:0ec5dc39dacf] Feature-wise transformation addresses a different embedding problem: domain-induced feature-distribution shift. Its mechanism inserts feature-wise affine modulation layers into the encoder so that training can simulate varied feature distributions; because manually tuning the transformation hyper-parameters can be difficult, the paper uses a learning-to-learn procedure to optimize those layers for performance on unseen domains. The authors describe the layers as method-agnostic add-ons for metric-based few-shot methods. This distinguishes it from K-tuplet or Proto-Triplet: those losses mainly reshape semantic geometry, whereas feature-wise transformation mainly diversifies activation statistics so the downstream metric is less specialized to seen-domain distributions. Its evidence and boundary are specifically tied to cross-domain few-shot classification; it is not presented as a replacement for the class representation or comparator. [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:2:ada74c4d4774:claim:83310823f8ec] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:aafe927bcc74] Contextual and multi-level embeddings move beyond a single image-independent encoder. QSFormer jointly models support and query images with a global sample Transformer branch, using encoder, decoder, and cross-attention components for support representation, query representation, and metric learning between the sets; a local patch Transformer captures long-range dependence among patches, and the Cross-scale Interactive Feature Extractor fuses multi-scale CNN features. MSENet instead uses a multi-output embedding network that extracts features at several stages, adds self-attention at each stage, and learns stage weights so that global, abstract, and shallower features all contribute. These methods are best understood as embedding-and-comparison hybrids: their attention can cross the support–query boundary, so the representation is already task-conditioned before a conventional distance or classifier is applied. The sources support effectiveness claims on standard and cross-domain benchmarks, but exact comparisons must wait for matched experiments because architecture, backbone, and protocol differ. [E:arxiv:2208.12398:abstract:claim:eb85178b6852] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:baa36cba9b0a]

Nearest-example class representation is the simplest support-set model: each labeled support image remains a separate reference, and a query is classified from its distances or similarities to those examples. Siamese and Matching-Network-style systems belong to this early pointwise comparison family in the reviewed survey. Its advantage is that no class-level summary has to be estimated from one to five images, avoiding prototype estimation error. Its limitation is equally direct: scarce and noisy support examples provide weak coverage of a novel class, and every support image can attract or repel a query without a model of within-class variation. This motivates class representations that aggregate the support set. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_few_shot_deep_metric_learning_methods:0:c53378070ee7:claim:f4690eeeb5d0] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1] Point-prototype methods summarize each class with one reference vector. In the basic form, support embeddings of a class are averaged into a prototype and queries are assigned to nearby prototypes under a fixed distance; prototypes may also be weighted averages or learned end to end to improve representational capacity. This converts variable numbers of support images into one stable class model and is the canonical bridge between embedding learning and distance-based classification. The method is attractive when support examples approximately form one compact cluster, but a single mean can hide multimodality, pose variation, outliers, and spatial structure. Shot count also matters: the same prototype rule can behave differently when the number of shots used in meta-training and meta-testing does not match, which is the specific hyperparameter sensitivity analyzed in the Prototypical-Network shot-number study. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:1909.11722:abstract:claim:ad5a8d7aede4] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:32d2f0aedf14] Distribution-based prototypes replace the point estimate with uncertainty about the class. Variational few-shot learning estimates a distribution for each class and can assign a query by a distributional measure such as Kullback–Leibler divergence, while also providing a confidence estimate for the class assignment. ABHFA-Net similarly models class prototypes as probability distributions and compares them with Bhattacharyya distance; it adds spatial-channel attention and a Bhattacharyya-based contrastive softmax loss for separability. These mechanisms are suited to few-shot conditions because they acknowledge that a few samples do not identify an exact class location. Their evidence is domain-specific: the survey reports the variational motivation in general few-shot image classification, whereas ABHFA-Net reports benchmark and disaster-image results, including 80.7% and 92.3% accuracy on CIFAR-FS 5-way 1-shot and 5-shot tasks and up to 68.2% and 78.3% on AIDER; those numbers should not be compared with methods that were not evaluated under the same disaster-data protocol. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:32d2f0aedf14] [E:arxiv:2510.18326:abstract:claim:2c570434b933] Subspace representations encode geometric span rather than a mean point or scalar uncertainty. Deep Subspace Network builds a low-dimensional subspace for each class from support samples through singular value decomposition and classifies a query by the shortest Euclidean distance between the query and its projection onto a class-specific subspace; the review states that this is more robust to noise and outliers than Prototypical Network. SRL extends the vector-to-subspace shift in local CNN feature space: an image is represented by a subspace, similarity is measured by weighted subspace distance, and K-shot classes can be summarized by prototypical or discriminative template subspaces. Its authors argue that subspaces preserve spatial structure and within-image diversity better than global vectors. SRL reports competitive or superior performance on MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, and CUB, but the strength of that claim depends on the paper's particular backbone and episode settings rather than establishing universal superiority of subspaces over prototypes. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:32d2f0aedf14] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8969ee1e4e70]

Fixed-distance classifiers use a pre-specified relation such as Euclidean or cosine distance after embeddings and class summaries are formed. Their contribution is not a learned comparator; the learning pressure resides in the encoder, support aggregation, normalization, temperature, or prototype construction. They are comparatively simple and make the decision rule easy to inspect, but they assume that a single geometric relation is appropriate across tasks and features. The Meta-Metric-Learner paper states this assumption explicitly: metric-based approaches can accommodate varying numbers of classes, but a task-invariant metric is easier to justify when tasks come from similar domains. Thus fixed distance is a useful baseline or component, not evidence that learned comparison is unnecessary. [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:1:74ed040863a6:claim:3812293ab161] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:0b0752f4ac3d] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:d539e10e3cd6] Learned-similarity methods train a comparator to map a query–support or query–class pair into a relation score instead of relying on Euclidean or cosine geometry. Relation Network is the standard example in the sources: a neural network learns the comparison and outputs class-related scores through episodic training. Region Comparison Network retains this learned-comparison idea at a finer spatial level, comparing regions between query and support images; its Region Activation Mapping visualizes intermediate comparisons and can generalize task-level explanations toward category-level prototypical parts. These methods can learn nonlinear, attribute-dependent matches that a fixed distance may miss, especially when local correspondence matters. Their trade-off is extra parameters and less direct interpretation as a mathematical metric; a high relation score is a learned compatibility estimate, not necessarily a distance satisfying metric axioms. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:efa61445b15c] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:0fa86bc29e24] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:8ddae53d33c7] MACO makes the break from a true metric explicit. Rather than comparing query and class representations in a metric space, it uses a parameterized network to output a softmax probability distribution; the authors therefore call the architecture metric-agnostic. Their ablation-oriented claim is stronger than merely replacing the distance: MACO performs best when class representations are conditioned on the target query, allowing attribute importance to vary according to the query–class interaction. It should be compared with metric-learning approaches as a relational or conditional classifier, but not mislabeled as a fixed-distance or even necessarily metric-based method. Its role in this review is to show that strong few-shot performance can arise from learned query-conditioned comparison, while also testing whether predefined metric spaces are essential. [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:2:c37dc575d3c8:claim:d5aad7ce0ffb] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:1:74ed040863a6:claim:3812293ab161] Task-adaptive metric learners modify the comparison machinery for each episode. Meta-Metric-Learner combines a task-specific metric-based base learner with a meta-learner that specifies the base model; the stated motivation is to retain the ability of metric methods to handle flexible class counts while generating metrics that generalize better across tasks, including single-source and multi-source settings with non-uniform class numbers. This differs from simply using a stronger universal encoder because the metric itself is conditioned or selected for the task. An adaptive metric is particularly relevant when task variance is high; for example, the natural-language few-shot paper in the sources argues that one metric cannot capture complex task variation and therefore learns a weighted combination of metrics. That language evidence is outside image classification, so it supports the general motivation for adaptive metrics but not an image-performance claim. [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:0b0752f4ac3d] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:d539e10e3cd6] [E:arxiv:1805.07513:abstract:claim:a72fdd6bb5c7] Relation learning can also be organized at several sample granularities. The multi-level relation method for cross-domain few-shot hyperspectral classification builds on a domain-discriminator approach but adds contrastive learning for class-level sample relations and a Transformer cross-attention module for set-level relations from queries to supports. It therefore addresses both domain discrepancy and the fact that direct query-to-prototype distances do not fully exploit relationships among samples. This is an application-specific metric-learning architecture rather than a natural-image benchmark method; its mechanism is relevant to the comparison, but its quantitative evidence belongs to hyperspectral tasks and should not be merged with mini-ImageNet or CUB rankings. [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:430d78b68501] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:3e17d5d5f5a5]

Hybrid metric-and-transfer methods broaden how the embedding is obtained. ProtoTransfer first uses self-supervised learning to construct a metric embedding in which unlabeled prototypical samples and their augmentations cluster closely; it then summarizes class clusters and fine-tunes for few-shot classification. The source reports that ProtoTransfer outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised meta-learning methods on mini-ImageNet and, under domain shift, achieves comparable performance to supervised methods while requiring orders of magnitude fewer labels. This is not a purely episodic supervised metric learner: its key contribution is the label-efficient pretraining route followed by prototype-style classification. It is comparable to other metric methods only when label budget, pretraining data, and whether fine-tuning is allowed are treated as first-class experimental conditions. [E:arxiv:2006.11325:abstract:claim:d76dc15743ab] Strong transfer-learning baselines complicate the boundary of metric-only comparisons. A standard cross-entropy-pretrained deep network, when fine-tuned on the few target labels and especially when fine-tuned transductively, is reported to outperform then-current state-of-the-art systems on Mini-ImageNet, Tiered-ImageNet, CIFAR-FS, and FC-100 under the same hyper-parameters, and the same paper demonstrates results on ImageNet-21k. This does not make the model a metric-learning mechanism; rather, it shows that benchmark gains attributed to episodic metric machinery must be separated from gains caused by representation pretraining and adaptation. For method comparison, a metric learner should therefore be evaluated against a well-specified fine-tuning baseline whenever the deployment setting permits target-label optimization. [E:arxiv:1909.02729:abstract:claim:5f189919bcf6] Interpretability-oriented metric learning changes the evidence a comparator can provide. RCN's region comparisons and RAM visualizations are intended to reveal which query and support regions correspond and contribute to a decision, including category-level prototypical parts. This is a different objective from improving the distance alone: it offers spatial explanations but does not automatically guarantee higher accuracy or causal validity of the visualized regions. Likewise, distributional methods can provide assignment confidence, and fixed-distance methods offer simpler geometric diagnostics. These properties should be treated as separate method characteristics rather than folded into a single accuracy ranking. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:0fa86bc29e24] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:32d2f0aedf14] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:1:74ed040863a6:claim:3812293ab161] Across these approaches, the central trade-off is structural complexity versus the information that can be recovered from a few supports. Embedding losses and feature modulation improve what is compared; nearest examples, prototypes, distributions, and subspaces change how a class is represented; fixed, learned, conditional, and task-adaptive comparators change how similarity is decided. Many concrete systems combine stages, so the most faithful method comparison is not a linear progression from simple to advanced but a matched analysis of encoder assumptions, support-set geometry, comparator flexibility, task/domain conditioning, and label usage. The next section therefore reports results only where datasets, episodes, backbones, and baselines are sufficiently aligned and leaves unmatched settings as non-comparable. ## Comparative Evidence Analysis

Experimental comparison rules. The metric-learning evidence should be read along four matched dimensions rather than as one leaderboard: the task split (in-domain versus cross-domain), the episode definition (K-way, n-shot and whether train/test shot counts match), the learned component (embedding, class representation, or comparator), and the protocol (backbone, pretraining, transductive or inductive inference, baselines, and metric). The reviewed survey organizes methods by those metric-learning stages and notes that metric learning can be combined with episodic meta-learning; therefore two models with similar accuracy are not directly comparable if one changes only a loss and another changes the backbone, support aggregation, or adaptation setting. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb]

The common in-domain image benchmark is an episode whose support and query classes are novel classes drawn from the same benchmark family used to construct meta-training tasks. MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, CIFAR-FS, FC-100, and CUB recur in the sources, but a dataset name alone is not enough for a fair comparison because class splits, backbones, image resolutions, pretraining, and query counts can differ. Cross-domain evaluation is a separate condition: the deep K-tuplet paper trains on miniImageNet and tests on Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, and Stanford Cars, while the feature-wise-transformation paper explicitly studies metric functions that may overfit feature distributions from seen domains. Thus a same-domain win and a cross-domain win answer different questions. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:53d7fbe2de7c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:22bea6df5855] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:aafe927bcc74] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:2:ada74c4d4774:claim:83310823f8ec]

Embedding-loss evidence is strongest when interpreted as evidence about representation geometry, not as a universal ranking of all metric methods. Deep K-tuplet changes the ordinary triplet objective by comparing each query jointly with K negatives and adds semi-hard mining; its paper reports that this feature-embedding baseline outperforms other metric-based methods on miniImageNet and, more distinctively, gives better cross-dataset transfer from miniImageNet to Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, and Stanford Cars. Proto-Triplet and ICNN instead enforce intra-class compactness and inter-class separation through modified triplet and nearest-neighbor losses; their paper reports about a 2 percentage-point accuracy improvement over compared metric-based methods on miniImageNet and competitive Caltech/CUB/Dogs/Cars generalization. Because the available excerpts do not provide identical backbones and shot-level tables for both papers, the supported comparison is that both target transferable embeddings, while their exact relative accuracy is not established here. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:abe1e207bc9c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:53d7fbe2de7c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:307bf74255b7] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:2b40d78bb79f]

Feature-wise transformation provides a controlled cross-domain contrast with embedding losses: K-tuplet and Proto-Triplet mainly alter semantic distances through training objectives, whereas transformation layers perturb encoder activations to simulate multiple feature distributions and are described as method-agnostic add-ons for metric-based few-shot models. The appropriate experimental question is therefore not simply whether the transformed model has higher miniImageNet accuracy, but whether inserting the same modulation into a fixed metric pipeline improves unseen-domain accuracy relative to that pipeline without modulation. The source supports the mechanism and cross-domain motivation, but the excerpt does not supply a complete numeric table, so no numerical ranking against K-tuplet, ICNN, or subspace methods can be inferred. [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:2:ada74c4d4774:claim:83310823f8ec] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:aafe927bcc74] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:abe1e207bc9c] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:2b40d78bb79f]

Class-representation comparisons separate point, distribution, and subspace assumptions. Point prototypes summarize support examples as one vector and are natural baselines when support images form a compact cluster; the shot-number study shows that the number of shots used in meta-training is a material hyperparameter for Prototypical Networks and that mismatched meta-training and meta-testing shot counts can affect performance. Distribution models instead estimate class uncertainty: ABHFA-Net models prototypes as probability distributions, compares them by Bhattacharyya distance, and reports 80.7% and 92.3% accuracy on CIFAR-FS 5-way 1-shot and 5-shot tasks, respectively. Those values are tied to ABHFA-Net's attention encoder, loss, backbone, and CIFAR-FS protocol; they cannot be used to rank it against a prototype method evaluated only on miniImageNet or with another architecture. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:1909.11722:abstract:claim:ad5a8d7aede4] [E:arxiv:2510.18326:abstract:claim:2c570434b933]

Subspace methods test whether geometric span is a better support-set summary than a mean vector under matched settings. Deep Subspace Network constructs a class-specific low-dimensional subspace by singular value decomposition and assigns a query to the class with the shortest distance from the query to its projected subspace; the review reports greater robustness to noise and outliers than Prototypical Network. SRL represents images or K-shot template classes as subspaces in local CNN feature space, uses weighted subspace distance, and reports competitive or superior performance on MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, and CUB. The comparison is meaningful against point prototypes because both use support geometry for classification, but the available excerpts do not provide matched means, confidence intervals, backbones, and per-shot numbers across DSN, SRL, and Prototypical Networks; consequently they support a qualitative geometry comparison, not a blanket accuracy ordering. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:32d2f0aedf14] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8969ee1e4e70]

Learned comparators should be compared on whether the comparator itself adds value after the encoder and class model are controlled. Relation-style networks replace a predefined Euclidean or cosine rule with a learned compatibility scorer; RCN performs region-level query–support comparison and reports effectiveness over existing baselines on four benchmark datasets, while also providing Region Activation Mapping explanations. MACO goes further and is explicitly metric-agnostic: a neural network outputs softmax probabilities and class representations are conditioned on the query. The evidence therefore distinguishes RCN's local, interpretable similarity learning from MACO's query-conditioned neural classifier, but neither excerpt supplies a common numeric table with the same backbone and episodes, so their accuracies cannot be ranked against each other or against fixed-distance prototypes from these snippets alone. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:0fa86bc29e24] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:8ddae53d33c7] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:2:c37dc575d3c8:claim:d5aad7ce0ffb] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:1:74ed040863a6:claim:3812293ab161]

Task-adaptive and contextual models broaden the experimental unit from one image pair to the whole episode. Meta-Metric-Learner combines a task-specific metric learner with a meta-learner that specifies the base model and evaluates standard episodes plus settings with flexible class counts in single-source and multi-source forms; this is a different stress test from the usual fixed 5-way protocol. QSFormer uses global query–support attention and local patch Transformers, while MSENet combines multi-stage embeddings, self-attention, and learned stage weights. These systems can improve representation and comparison jointly, which means an accuracy gain cannot be attributed solely to a better metric. Their results are comparable only to baselines re-run with matched backbones, attention modules, training data, and episode settings. [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:0b0752f4ac3d] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:d539e10e3cd6] [E:arxiv:2208.12398:abstract:claim:eb85178b6852] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:baa36cba9b0a]

Non-episodic and label-budget baselines are essential controls because apparent metric-learning gains may come from representation pretraining. The fine-tuning study reports that a network pretrained with standard cross-entropy and fine-tuned, especially transductively, outperforms then-current state-of-the-art methods on Mini-ImageNet, Tiered-ImageNet, CIFAR-FS, and FC-100 with the same hyper-parameters, and it also reports ImageNet-21k experiments. ProtoTransfer uses self-supervised prototype-style transfer and reports better performance than state-of-the-art unsupervised meta-learning methods on mini-ImageNet and comparable supervised-domain-shift performance with orders of magnitude fewer labels. These are not like-for-like comparisons with supervised inductive metric learners unless pretraining data, labels, and fine-tuning/transduction are matched; they do, however, show that a metric method must beat a strong embedding-and-fine-tuning baseline under the intended deployment regime. [E:arxiv:1909.02729:abstract:claim:5f189919bcf6] [E:arxiv:2006.11325:abstract:claim:d76dc15743ab]

Domain-specific benchmarks and unmatched results should remain separate from natural-image rankings. The FewSAR benchmark reimplements 15 classic methods in three categories under common SAR protocols and reports that, within that benchmark, metric-learning methods attain the best accuracy while meta-learning and fine-tuning methods perform poorly, with the authors attributing that pattern partly to biases of existing SAR datasets. The hyperspectral multi-level relation method adds class-level contrastive and set-level cross-attention relations and demonstrates gains over state-of-the-art methods in cross-domain few-shot hyperspectral classification. ABHFA-Net also reports disaster-image results, including up to 68.2% 1-shot and 78.3% 5-shot accuracy on AIDER. These findings support applicability in their respective sensor domains, but they are non-comparable with miniImageNet or CUB numbers and do not establish a universal ordering of metric-learning mechanisms. [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:616f72ed5776] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:430d78b68501] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:3e17d5d5f5a5] [E:arxiv:2510.18326:abstract:claim:2c570434b933]

## Limitations and Open Problems

Open problems and trade-offs. The first unresolved issue is that the three-stage decomposition—embedding, class representation, and comparator—does not imply that gains can be cleanly attributed to one stage. Many metric learners train an encoder, support-set aggregation, and nonlinear relation module end to end, while contextual Transformers or attention models can simultaneously alter image features and query–support interactions. As a result, an accuracy improvement over a simpler prototype baseline may come from a stronger backbone, additional parameters, task conditioning, or the comparison rule rather than from the metric idea alone. Future comparisons need controlled ablations that hold the encoder, training data, episode sampler, optimizer, augmentation, and inference mode fixed before claiming that a particular distance or class model is responsible. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2208.12398:abstract:claim:eb85178b6852] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:baa36cba9b0a]

A second problem is the fragility of class summaries estimated from one to five examples. Nearest-example comparisons avoid averaging but can be dominated by a noisy support image; a mean prototype is compact but assumes an approximately unimodal cluster and can erase pose, viewpoint, or part-level variation; distribution and subspace models express uncertainty or geometric span but still estimate those structures from very few samples. The reported robustness of subspace methods to noise and outliers is therefore conditional rather than a reason to discard prototypes. The practical implication is that no single support-set geometry is guaranteed to match every task: benchmark comparisons should include controlled support noise, outlier supports, multimodal classes, and varying shot counts rather than reporting only standard 1-shot and 5-shot means. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:32d2f0aedf14] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8969ee1e4e70]

Shot-count mismatch remains a concrete protocol problem. The Prototypical-Network analysis identifies the number of shots used during meta-training as a crucial hyperparameter and notes that performance is generally best when meta-training and meta-testing shot counts agree. This matters because many papers train on a fixed 5-way 1-shot or 5-shot objective and then present results for both settings, potentially conflating the quality of a class representation with favorable episode sampling. Methods should report performance when training shot count differs from deployment shot count, and ideally evaluate across a range of support-set sizes rather than treating 1-shot and 5-shot as isolated tasks. [E:arxiv:1909.11722:abstract:claim:ad5a8d7aede4]

Cross-domain generalization is not solved by in-domain episodic accuracy. The feature-wise-transformation paper motivates its method by observing that feature distributions differ across domains and that a metric function can overfit statistics seen during training; the deep K-tuplet and Proto-Triplet/ICNN papers respond mainly through embedding objectives and evaluate transfer from miniImageNet to datasets such as CUB, Dogs, Cars, and Caltech. These are complementary responses, but the evidence is tied to particular source–target pairs. A model that transfers to four natural-image datasets may still fail under sensor shift, remote-sensing imagery, disaster scenes, or hyperspectral data, so cross-domain claims should specify the source domain, target domains, label budget, and whether target data were used for tuning. [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:aafe927bcc74] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:2:ada74c4d4774:claim:83310823f8ec] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:abe1e207bc9c] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:2b40d78bb79f] [E:arxiv:2510.18326:abstract:claim:2c570434b933] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:430d78b68501]

The boundary between metric learning and strong representation learning is also still unsettled. A standard cross-entropy-pretrained network with careful fine-tuning, particularly transductive fine-tuning, is reported to outperform then-current few-shot systems on Mini-ImageNet, Tiered-ImageNet, CIFAR-FS, and FC-100 under the same hyper-parameters. ProtoTransfer further shows that self-supervised prototype-style transfer can be label-efficient and competitive under domain shift. These findings do not invalidate learned metrics, but they show that metric papers must separate the value of pretraining and target-label adaptation from the value of episodic similarity learning. Without such controls, leaderboard gains may overstate the contribution of the metric component. [E:arxiv:1909.02729:abstract:claim:5f189919bcf6] [E:arxiv:2006.11325:abstract:claim:d76dc15743ab]

Learned comparators introduce their own interpretability and identifiability trade-off. Fixed Euclidean or cosine distances are easy to inspect but may be too rigid across tasks; neural relation scores can model nonlinear, attribute-dependent matches, but a soft relation score need not satisfy metric axioms. MACO makes this explicit by replacing metric-space comparison with a query-conditioned neural classifier, and RCN addresses interpretability through region comparisons and activation maps. RCN-style visualizations are useful evidence about correspondence, but they do not by themselves prove that the highlighted regions causally determine the prediction. Comparator research therefore needs both metric-agnostic controls and explanation tests beyond visualization, such as perturbation or part-occlusion evaluations. [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:1:74ed040863a6:claim:3812293ab161] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:2:c37dc575d3c8:claim:d5aad7ce0ffb] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:0fa86bc29e24] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:8ddae53d33c7]

Task adaptation creates a flexibility–complexity trade-off. A task-invariant metric is simple and can handle different class counts, but the Meta-Metric-Learner paper argues that one metric is strained when tasks have flexible class numbers or come from less similar domains; task-specific metrics, query-conditioned representations, and attention over the full episode can adapt to those conditions. The cost is additional meta-learning machinery, greater dependence on the task distribution used during training, and more difficulty diagnosing whether adaptation improves semantic comparison or merely fits episode statistics. Adaptive methods should therefore be evaluated on held-out task structures, varying way counts, and domains not represented when the adaptation rule was learned, rather than only on fixed 5-way episodes. [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:0b0752f4ac3d] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:d539e10e3cd6] [E:arxiv:2208.12398:abstract:claim:eb85178b6852]

Benchmark heterogeneity continues to impede reliable ranking. The reviewed sources use MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, CIFAR-FS, FC-100, CUB, Caltech, Dogs, Cars, SAR, hyperspectral, and disaster datasets with different backbones, splits, supervision budgets, and application assumptions. FewSAR explicitly notes that SAR research has suffered from non-unified datasets and custom experimental setups, and it addresses this by providing common protocols and runtime analysis; domain-specific studies such as ABHFA-Net and the hyperspectral relation model report strong results in their own settings. Those numbers cannot be merged into a universal metric-learning leaderboard. The field needs common code, matched baselines, uncertainty estimates, runtime or parameter reporting, and separate leaderboards for in-domain, cross-domain natural-image, transductive, unsupervised, and sensor-specific tasks. [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:616f72ed5776] [E:arxiv:2510.18326:abstract:claim:2c570434b933] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:430d78b68501] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1]

Efficiency and deployment constraints are under-specified in much of the metric-learning evidence. Subspace construction, distribution estimation, multi-stage encoders, cross-attention, graph or Transformer relation modules, and task-specific metric adaptation may improve accuracy but add computation, memory, or tuning requirements. Conversely, a simple fixed-distance prototype can be inexpensive at inference but may underfit complex support structure. The FewSAR benchmark is distinctive in the selected sources because it analyzes both quantitative results and runtime under a common setting; most natural-image excerpts reviewed here do not provide enough matched latency, memory, parameter-count, or tuning-cost evidence. Accuracy alone therefore cannot determine which metric approach is preferable in a data-scarce, time-critical application. [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:616f72ed5776] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e] [E:arxiv:2208.12398:abstract:claim:eb85178b6852] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:baa36cba9b0a] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:0b0752f4ac3d]

Finally, scope discipline remains important. Few-shot metric learning is related to, but not identical to, optimization-based meta-learning, transfer learning, zero-shot recognition, and domain-specific classification. Zero-shot methods compare images with semantic attributes or class descriptions without labeled support examples, whereas few-shot metric methods compare against support examples or class models; natural-language adaptive-metric evidence may motivate task-adaptive image methods but does not establish image accuracy; and SAR or hyperspectral results demonstrate application fit rather than universal superiority. The most useful future work would preserve these distinctions while reporting matched ablations, cross-domain stress tests, label and compute budgets, and uncertainty, so that embedding, representation, and comparator contributions can be compared without turning method-specific evidence into an unsupported global ranking. ## Conclusion

The direct comparison favors a matched-component view rather than a single ranking: simple prototypes and fixed distances remain transparent baselines, while richer class models and learned comparators are justified only when matched evidence shows they address support noise, multimodality, local correspondence or task variation. Hybrid contextual models complicate attribution because they change features and comparison jointly. report.html:
Metric Learning for Few-Shot Image Classification: An Embedding–Representation–Metric Comparison

Abstract

Metric-learning few-shot classifiers are best compared by where their main bias acts: the encoder, the support-set class model, or the comparison rule. Embedding losses and modulation target transferable features; nearest examples, prototypes, distributions and subspaces encode support information differently; fixed, learned, query-conditioned and task-adaptive comparators vary decision flexibility. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:0fa86bc29e24] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:0b0752f4ac3d] [E:arxiv:2006.11325:abstract:claim:d76dc15743ab] Reported gains do not support one universal winner. K-tuplet and Proto-Triplet/ICNN show embedding and cross-dataset benefits, distribution and subspace methods address uncertainty or geometry, and RCN or MACO add learned relational comparison, but results differ in backbone, shots, datasets, pretraining, inference and label budget. In-domain, cross-domain, sensor-domain and label-efficient transfer settings must therefore be compared separately. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:abe1e207bc9c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:53d7fbe2de7c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:22bea6df5855] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:307bf74255b7] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:2b40d78bb79f] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:0ec5dc39dacf] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:32d2f0aedf14] [E:arxiv:2510.18326:abstract:claim:2c570434b933] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8969ee1e4e70] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:efa61445b15c] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:0fa86bc29e24] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:8ddae53d33c7] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:2:c37dc575d3c8:claim:d5aad7ce0ffb] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:1:74ed040863a6:claim:3812293ab161] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:aafe927bcc74] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:2:ada74c4d4774:claim:83310823f8ec] [E:arxiv:1909.02729:abstract:claim:5f189919bcf6] [E:arxiv:2006.11325:abstract:claim:d76dc15743ab] [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:616f72ed5776] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:430d78b68501] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:3e17d5d5f5a5]

Introduction

Few-shot image classification asks a model to assign query images to classes when each novel class supplies only a small labeled support set, commonly one to five examples. The central difficulty is that ordinary supervised training can overfit to these few labels; metric-learning approaches respond by learning an embedding space and/or a similarity function in which same-class samples are close and different-class samples are far apart, then classifying a query by its relation to support samples or aggregated class representations. This review therefore compares approaches by the stage at which their main inductive bias operates: the image embedding, the class representation, and the distance or comparison rule. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:0fa86bc29e24] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1]

The standard episode makes the comparison structure explicit: a support set contains the few labeled images for the task's classes, and a query set contains unlabeled images from those classes. A feature encoder maps both sets into an embedding space, after which a metric function compares query features with support examples or class models to produce predictions. This framing covers nearest-example methods, prototype methods, distribution or subspace models, and learned relation networks, while excluding methods whose main mechanism is gradient-based task adaptation rather than comparison in a learned space. [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:aafe927bcc74] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:efa61445b15c]

The organizing choice used here is the review's three-stage grouping—learning feature embeddings, learning class representations, and learning distance measures—rather than a universal taxonomy. These dimensions are complementary: one method may improve the encoder, another may replace a mean prototype with a distribution or subspace, and a third may replace a fixed Euclidean or cosine comparison with a learned relation model. Metric learning can also be trained episodically as meta-learning, so the labels “metric-based” and “meta-learning” are not mutually exclusive. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb]

The comparison must also distinguish in-domain from cross-domain evaluation. In the familiar mini-ImageNet-style protocol, base and novel classes are drawn from the same benchmark domain; in cross-domain few-shot learning, the model is trained on one source domain, such as mini-ImageNet, and tested on novel classes from datasets such as CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, Stanford Cars, or Caltech-101. Consequently, accuracy under same-domain episodes does not by itself establish robustness to domain shift, and later sections keep datasets, shots, backbones, baselines, and training settings together before drawing any comparative conclusion. [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:aafe927bcc74] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:53d7fbe2de7c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:22bea6df5855]

Background and Method Taxonomy

Taxonomy used in this review. The methods are organized by the three metric-learning stages identified in the reviewed survey: learning feature embeddings, learning class representations, and learning distance or similarity measures. This is an analytical grouping for comparing mechanisms, not a claim that every paper uses these labels or that a model belongs to only one stage. A single architecture can contribute at several stages—for example, an episodic encoder, an aggregated prototype, and a learned relation module can be trained end to end. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb]

Embedding-centered approaches place most of the model's adaptation burden on the feature map. Their premise is that a discriminative, task-general embedding should pull same-class images together and push different-class images apart before the final comparison. Examples in the sources include Siamese-style and triplet-like embedding learning, deep K-tuplet learning with multiple negatives, task-specific feature transformers or modulation, self-attention or multi-stage embeddings, and query–support Transformers that refine representations using context from the whole episode. These methods still need a decision rule, but their main novelty is what counts as a comparable feature and whether features are task-agnostic or task-conditioned. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_few_shot_deep_metric_learning_methods:0:c53378070ee7:claim:f4690eeeb5d0] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:abe1e207bc9c] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:2:ada74c4d4774:claim:83310823f8ec] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:baa36cba9b0a] [E:arxiv:2208.12398:abstract:claim:eb85178b6852]

Class-representation approaches differ in how the few support examples summarize a class. Early nearest-example methods compare a query directly with individual support embeddings. Point-prototype methods replace that set of comparisons with a reference vector, typically a simple or weighted mean of support features. Distributional and subspace approaches instead model uncertainty or geometric structure: variational representations estimate class distributions and can use KL divergence, Deep Subspace Network represents each class by a low-dimensional subspace and assigns a query by nearest projected distance, while SRL represents images or class templates as subspaces in local CNN feature space. The relevant distinction is therefore not merely “prototype versus non-prototype,” but whether a class is encoded as isolated points, one vector, a distribution, or a subspace. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:32d2f0aedf14] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8969ee1e4e70]

Distance-centered approaches vary the comparison rule after features and class summaries are formed. Fixed-rule methods use a predefined relation such as Euclidean or cosine distance. Learned-similarity methods train a network to score query–support or query–prototype pairs; Relation Network and Region Comparison Network fall in this broad family, with RCN additionally designed to expose corresponding image regions through its comparison and visualization mechanism. A further distinction is that a learned comparator producing class scores is not necessarily a mathematical metric: MACO explicitly replaces metric-space comparison with a neural classifier and conditions class representations on the query, so its authors describe it as metric-agnostic rather than a true metric-learning method. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:efa61445b15c] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:0fa86bc29e24] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:8ddae53d33c7] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:2:c37dc575d3c8:claim:d5aad7ce0ffb] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:1:74ed040863a6:claim:3812293ab161]

Task conditioning supplies another useful comparison axis. A task-invariant metric assumes one embedding and comparison rule can transfer across episodes from a similar domain, whereas task-specific methods adapt features, metrics, or class representations to the current support set. The Meta-Metric-Learner paper motivates this split by arguing that a single task-invariant metric is strained when tasks contain varying class counts or come from less similar domains; it combines a task-specific metric learner with a meta-learner that specifies the base model. Likewise, cross-domain feature-wise modulation targets distribution shift by perturbing encoder activations during training so the downstream metric is less tied to seen-domain feature statistics. These axes cut across the three-stage taxonomy: conditioning may be implemented in the encoder, class model, comparator, or a hybrid meta-model. [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:0b0752f4ac3d] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:d539e10e3cd6] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:2:ada74c4d4774:claim:83310823f8ec] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:aafe927bcc74]

Boundaries and adjacent objectives. Metric-based few-shot classification should be distinguished from optimization-based meta-learning, whose central mechanism is learning an initialization or update rule for task-specific parameters, and from ordinary transfer learning or fine-tuning, where a source-pretrained classifier is adapted to target labels. These paradigms can overlap: metric embeddings may be learned through episodic meta-training, and self-supervised or transfer-trained embeddings may later be used with prototypes. The taxonomy also should not be confused with zero-shot recognition, which compares images to semantic class descriptions or attributes rather than to a few labeled support images, or with domain-specific applications such as SAR and hyperspectral classification, where metric learning is a method rather than a separate task definition. Efficiency, interpretability, and cross-domain robustness are evaluation objectives or design constraints; they do not by themselves define a separate metric-learning family. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:efa61445b15c] [E:arxiv:2006.11325:abstract:claim:d76dc15743ab] [E:arxiv:1607.08085:abstract:claim:062328880b00] [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:616f72ed5776] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:430d78b68501]

Representative Methods

Embedding-first metric learners treat the encoder as the main learned component while keeping the final comparison relatively simple. Their common mechanism is to optimize a deep embedding so that images from the same class are mapped nearby and images from different classes are separated, then classify novel queries by nearest support examples, prototypes, or another distance-based rule. This family is appropriate when the central concern is transfer of visual features to unseen classes, but it does not remove the need to specify how support examples are aggregated or how distance is computed. The reviewed survey places embedding learning as the first of its three metric-learning stages and lists task-agnostic features, task-specific features, augmentation, multi-task learning, and semi-supervised variants within that broad stage. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_few_shot_deep_metric_learning_methods:0:c53378070ee7:claim:f4690eeeb5d0] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb] Deep K-tuplet Network makes the embedding objective more episode-like than an ordinary triplet loss. A standard triplet update compares an anchor with one positive and one negative, whereas few-shot episodes require a query to be discriminated from several competing classes; the K-tuplet formulation jointly compares against K negative samples in each mini-batch and uses semi-hard mining to select informative triplets, speed convergence, and stabilize training. Its authors present the method as a strong feature-embedding baseline and state that the learned embedding can be combined with a learnable non-linear distance metric. The evidence they claim is competitive mini-ImageNet performance relative to metric-based and other meta-based methods and stronger cross-dataset transfer when training on mini-ImageNet and testing on Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, and Stanford Cars. Its applicability boundary is that the reported cross-domain result concerns a model trained on mini-ImageNet and evaluated on those specific target datasets; it should not be generalized to arbitrary domain shifts without matched evaluation. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:abe1e207bc9c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:53d7fbe2de7c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:22bea6df5855] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:307bf74255b7] Proto-Triplet and the ICNN loss are later embedding-loss methods that explicitly constrain latent-space geometry rather than only optimizing episodic classification. Proto-Triplet adapts triplet-style optimization to the few-shot setting, while ICNN uses an inter-class and intra-class nearest-neighbor score to assess and improve embedding separability. The paper reports that these losses improved mini-ImageNet accuracy by about 2 percentage points over compared metric-based few-shot methods and also showed competitive generalization on Caltech, CUB, Dogs, and Cars. Because the available source states aggregate claims rather than the full backbone, shot-by-shot results, and training recipe, the supported conclusion is that the losses target embedding compactness and separation; a precise ranking against methods with different architectures or protocols is not warranted from this evidence alone. [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:2b40d78bb79f] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:0ec5dc39dacf] Feature-wise transformation addresses a different embedding problem: domain-induced feature-distribution shift. Its mechanism inserts feature-wise affine modulation layers into the encoder so that training can simulate varied feature distributions; because manually tuning the transformation hyper-parameters can be difficult, the paper uses a learning-to-learn procedure to optimize those layers for performance on unseen domains. The authors describe the layers as method-agnostic add-ons for metric-based few-shot methods. This distinguishes it from K-tuplet or Proto-Triplet: those losses mainly reshape semantic geometry, whereas feature-wise transformation mainly diversifies activation statistics so the downstream metric is less specialized to seen-domain distributions. Its evidence and boundary are specifically tied to cross-domain few-shot classification; it is not presented as a replacement for the class representation or comparator. [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:2:ada74c4d4774:claim:83310823f8ec] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:aafe927bcc74] Contextual and multi-level embeddings move beyond a single image-independent encoder. QSFormer jointly models support and query images with a global sample Transformer branch, using encoder, decoder, and cross-attention components for support representation, query representation, and metric learning between the sets; a local patch Transformer captures long-range dependence among patches, and the Cross-scale Interactive Feature Extractor fuses multi-scale CNN features. MSENet instead uses a multi-output embedding network that extracts features at several stages, adds self-attention at each stage, and learns stage weights so that global, abstract, and shallower features all contribute. These methods are best understood as embedding-and-comparison hybrids: their attention can cross the support–query boundary, so the representation is already task-conditioned before a conventional distance or classifier is applied. The sources support effectiveness claims on standard and cross-domain benchmarks, but exact comparisons must wait for matched experiments because architecture, backbone, and protocol differ. [E:arxiv:2208.12398:abstract:claim:eb85178b6852] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:baa36cba9b0a]

Nearest-example class representation is the simplest support-set model: each labeled support image remains a separate reference, and a query is classified from its distances or similarities to those examples. Siamese and Matching-Network-style systems belong to this early pointwise comparison family in the reviewed survey. Its advantage is that no class-level summary has to be estimated from one to five images, avoiding prototype estimation error. Its limitation is equally direct: scarce and noisy support examples provide weak coverage of a novel class, and every support image can attract or repel a query without a model of within-class variation. This motivates class representations that aggregate the support set. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_few_shot_deep_metric_learning_methods:0:c53378070ee7:claim:f4690eeeb5d0] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1] Point-prototype methods summarize each class with one reference vector. In the basic form, support embeddings of a class are averaged into a prototype and queries are assigned to nearby prototypes under a fixed distance; prototypes may also be weighted averages or learned end to end to improve representational capacity. This converts variable numbers of support images into one stable class model and is the canonical bridge between embedding learning and distance-based classification. The method is attractive when support examples approximately form one compact cluster, but a single mean can hide multimodality, pose variation, outliers, and spatial structure. Shot count also matters: the same prototype rule can behave differently when the number of shots used in meta-training and meta-testing does not match, which is the specific hyperparameter sensitivity analyzed in the Prototypical-Network shot-number study. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:1909.11722:abstract:claim:ad5a8d7aede4] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:32d2f0aedf14] Distribution-based prototypes replace the point estimate with uncertainty about the class. Variational few-shot learning estimates a distribution for each class and can assign a query by a distributional measure such as Kullback–Leibler divergence, while also providing a confidence estimate for the class assignment. ABHFA-Net similarly models class prototypes as probability distributions and compares them with Bhattacharyya distance; it adds spatial-channel attention and a Bhattacharyya-based contrastive softmax loss for separability. These mechanisms are suited to few-shot conditions because they acknowledge that a few samples do not identify an exact class location. Their evidence is domain-specific: the survey reports the variational motivation in general few-shot image classification, whereas ABHFA-Net reports benchmark and disaster-image results, including 80.7% and 92.3% accuracy on CIFAR-FS 5-way 1-shot and 5-shot tasks and up to 68.2% and 78.3% on AIDER; those numbers should not be compared with methods that were not evaluated under the same disaster-data protocol. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:32d2f0aedf14] [E:arxiv:2510.18326:abstract:claim:2c570434b933] Subspace representations encode geometric span rather than a mean point or scalar uncertainty. Deep Subspace Network builds a low-dimensional subspace for each class from support samples through singular value decomposition and classifies a query by the shortest Euclidean distance between the query and its projection onto a class-specific subspace; the review states that this is more robust to noise and outliers than Prototypical Network. SRL extends the vector-to-subspace shift in local CNN feature space: an image is represented by a subspace, similarity is measured by weighted subspace distance, and K-shot classes can be summarized by prototypical or discriminative template subspaces. Its authors argue that subspaces preserve spatial structure and within-image diversity better than global vectors. SRL reports competitive or superior performance on MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, and CUB, but the strength of that claim depends on the paper's particular backbone and episode settings rather than establishing universal superiority of subspaces over prototypes. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:32d2f0aedf14] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8969ee1e4e70]

Fixed-distance classifiers use a pre-specified relation such as Euclidean or cosine distance after embeddings and class summaries are formed. Their contribution is not a learned comparator; the learning pressure resides in the encoder, support aggregation, normalization, temperature, or prototype construction. They are comparatively simple and make the decision rule easy to inspect, but they assume that a single geometric relation is appropriate across tasks and features. The Meta-Metric-Learner paper states this assumption explicitly: metric-based approaches can accommodate varying numbers of classes, but a task-invariant metric is easier to justify when tasks come from similar domains. Thus fixed distance is a useful baseline or component, not evidence that learned comparison is unnecessary. [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:1:74ed040863a6:claim:3812293ab161] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:0b0752f4ac3d] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:d539e10e3cd6] Learned-similarity methods train a comparator to map a query–support or query–class pair into a relation score instead of relying on Euclidean or cosine geometry. Relation Network is the standard example in the sources: a neural network learns the comparison and outputs class-related scores through episodic training. Region Comparison Network retains this learned-comparison idea at a finer spatial level, comparing regions between query and support images; its Region Activation Mapping visualizes intermediate comparisons and can generalize task-level explanations toward category-level prototypical parts. These methods can learn nonlinear, attribute-dependent matches that a fixed distance may miss, especially when local correspondence matters. Their trade-off is extra parameters and less direct interpretation as a mathematical metric; a high relation score is a learned compatibility estimate, not necessarily a distance satisfying metric axioms. Rather than comparing query and class representations in a metric space, it uses a parameterized network to output a softmax probability distribution; the authors therefore call the architecture metric-agnostic. Their ablation-oriented claim is stronger than merely replacing the distance: MACO performs best when class representations are conditioned on the target query, allowing attribute importance to vary according to the query–class interaction. It should be compared with metric-learning approaches as a relational or conditional classifier, but not mislabeled as a fixed-distance or even necessarily metric-based method. Its role in this review is to show that strong few-shot performance can arise from learned query-conditioned comparison, while also testing whether predefined metric spaces are essential.
