Meta-Metric-Learner combines a task-specific metric-based base learner with a meta-learner that specifies the base model; the stated motivation is to retain the ability of metric methods to handle flexible class counts while generating metrics that generalize better across tasks, including single-source and multi-source settings with non-uniform class numbers. This differs from simply using a stronger universal encoder because the metric itself is conditioned or selected for the task. An adaptive metric is particularly relevant when task variance is high; for example, the natural-language few-shot paper in the sources argues that one metric cannot capture complex task variation and therefore learns a weighted combination of metrics. That language evidence is outside image classification, so it supports the general motivation for adaptive metrics but not an image-performance claim. Hybrid metric-and-transfer methods broaden how the embedding is obtained. ProtoTransfer first uses self-supervised learning to construct a metric embedding in which unlabeled prototypical samples and their augmentations cluster closely; it then summarizes class clusters and fine-tunes for few-shot classification. The source reports that ProtoTransfer outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised meta-learning methods on mini-ImageNet and, under domain shift, achieves comparable performance to supervised methods while requiring orders of magnitude fewer labels. This is not a purely episodic supervised metric learner: its key contribution is the label-efficient pretraining route followed by prototype-style classification. It is comparable to other metric methods only when label budget, pretraining data, and whether fine-tuning is allowed are treated as first-class experimental conditions. [E:arxiv:2006.11325:abstract:claim:d76dc15743ab] Strong transfer-learning baselines complicate the boundary of metric-only comparisons. A standard cross-entropy-pretrained deep network, when fine-tuned on the few target labels and especially when fine-tuned transductively, is reported to outperform then-current state-of-the-art systems on Mini-ImageNet, Tiered-ImageNet, CIFAR-FS, and FC-100 under the same hyper-parameters, and the same paper demonstrates results on ImageNet-21k. This does not make the model a metric-learning mechanism; rather, it shows that benchmark gains attributed to episodic metric machinery must be separated from gains caused by representation pretraining and adaptation. For method comparison, a metric learner should therefore be evaluated against a well-specified fine-tuning baseline whenever the deployment setting permits target-label optimization. [E:arxiv:1909.02729:abstract:claim:5f189919bcf6] Interpretability-oriented metric learning changes the evidence a comparator can provide. RCN's region comparisons and RAM visualizations are intended to reveal which query and support regions correspond and contribute to a decision, including category-level prototypical parts. This is a different objective from improving the distance alone: it offers spatial explanations but does not automatically guarantee higher accuracy or causal validity of the visualized regions. Likewise, distributional methods can provide assignment confidence, and fixed-distance methods offer simpler geometric diagnostics. These properties should be treated as separate method characteristics rather than folded into a single accuracy ranking. Embedding losses and feature modulation improve what is compared; nearest examples, prototypes, distributions, and subspaces change how a class is represented; fixed, learned, conditional, and task-adaptive comparators change how similarity is decided. Many concrete systems combine stages, so the most faithful method comparison is not a linear progression from simple to advanced but a matched analysis of encoder assumptions, support-set geometry, comparator flexibility, task/domain conditioning, and label usage. The next section therefore reports results only where datasets, episodes, backbones, and baselines are sufficiently aligned and leaves unmatched settings as non-comparable. Comparative Evidence Analysis

Experimental comparison rules. The metric-learning evidence should be read along four matched dimensions rather than as one leaderboard: the task split (in-domain versus cross-domain), the episode definition (K-way, n-shot and whether train/test shot counts match), the learned component (embedding, class representation, or comparator), and the protocol (backbone, pretraining, transductive or inductive inference, baselines, and metric). The reviewed survey organizes methods by those metric-learning stages and notes that metric learning can be combined with episodic meta-learning; therefore two models with similar accuracy are not directly comparable if one changes only a loss and another changes the backbone, support aggregation, or adaptation setting. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb]

The common in-domain image benchmark is an episode whose support and query classes are novel classes drawn from the same benchmark family used to construct meta-training tasks. MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, CIFAR-FS, FC-100, and CUB recur in the sources, but a dataset name alone is not enough for a fair comparison because class splits, backbones, image resolutions, pretraining, and query counts can differ. Cross-domain evaluation is a separate condition: the deep K-tuplet paper trains on miniImageNet and tests on Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, and Stanford Cars, while the feature-wise-transformation paper explicitly studies metric functions that may overfit feature distributions from seen domains. Thus a same-domain win and a cross-domain win answer different questions. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:53d7fbe2de7c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:22bea6df5855] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:aafe927bcc74] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:2:ada74c4d4774:claim:83310823f8ec]

Embedding-loss evidence is strongest when interpreted as evidence about representation geometry, not as a universal ranking of all metric methods. Deep K-tuplet changes the ordinary triplet objective by comparing each query jointly with K negatives and adds semi-hard mining; its paper reports that this feature-embedding baseline outperforms other metric-based methods on miniImageNet and, more distinctively, gives better cross-dataset transfer from miniImageNet to Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, and Stanford Cars. Proto-Triplet and ICNN instead enforce intra-class compactness and inter-class separation through modified triplet and nearest-neighbor losses; their paper reports about a 2 percentage-point accuracy improvement over compared metric-based methods on miniImageNet and competitive Caltech/CUB/Dogs/Cars generalization. Because the available excerpts do not provide identical backbones and shot-level tables for both papers, the supported comparison is that both target transferable embeddings, while their exact relative accuracy is not established here. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:abe1e207bc9c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:53d7fbe2de7c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:307bf74255b7] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:2b40d78bb79f]

Feature-wise transformation provides a controlled cross-domain contrast with embedding losses: K-tuplet and Proto-Triplet mainly alter semantic distances through training objectives, whereas transformation layers perturb encoder activations to simulate multiple feature distributions and are described as method-agnostic add-ons for metric-based few-shot models. The appropriate experimental question is therefore not simply whether the transformed model has higher miniImageNet accuracy, but whether inserting the same modulation into a fixed metric pipeline improves unseen-domain accuracy relative to that pipeline without modulation. The source supports the mechanism and cross-domain motivation, but the excerpt does not supply a complete numeric table, so no numerical ranking against K-tuplet, ICNN, or subspace methods can be inferred. [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:2:ada74c4d4774:claim:83310823f8ec] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:aafe927bcc74] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:abe1e207bc9c] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:2b40d78bb79f]

Class-representation comparisons separate point, distribution, and subspace assumptions. Point prototypes summarize support examples as one vector and are natural baselines when support images form a compact cluster; the shot-number study shows that the number of shots used in meta-training is a material hyperparameter for Prototypical Networks and that mismatched meta-training and meta-testing shot counts can affect performance. Distribution models instead estimate class uncertainty: ABHFA-Net models prototypes as probability distributions, compares them by Bhattacharyya distance, and reports 80.7% and 92.3% accuracy on CIFAR-FS 5-way 1-shot and 5-shot tasks, respectively. Those values are tied to ABHFA-Net's attention encoder, loss, backbone, and CIFAR-FS protocol; they cannot be used to rank it against a prototype method evaluated only on miniImageNet or with another architecture. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:1909.11722:abstract:claim:ad5a8d7aede4] [E:arxiv:2510.18326:abstract:claim:2c570434b933]

Subspace methods test whether geometric span is a better support-set summary than a mean vector under matched settings. Deep Subspace Network constructs a class-specific low-dimensional subspace by singular value decomposition and assigns a query to the class with the shortest distance from the query to its projected subspace; the review reports greater robustness to noise and outliers than Prototypical Network. SRL represents images or K-shot template classes as subspaces in local CNN feature space, uses weighted subspace distance, and reports competitive or superior performance on MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, and CUB. The comparison is meaningful against point prototypes because both use support geometry for classification, but the available excerpts do not provide matched means, confidence intervals, backbones, and per-shot numbers across DSN, SRL, and Prototypical Networks; consequently they support a qualitative geometry comparison, not a blanket accuracy ordering. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:32d2f0aedf14] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8969ee1e4e70]

Learned comparators should be compared on whether the comparator itself adds value after the encoder and class model are controlled. Relation-style networks replace a predefined Euclidean or cosine rule with a learned compatibility scorer; RCN performs region-level query–support comparison and reports effectiveness over existing baselines on four benchmark datasets, while also providing Region Activation Mapping explanations. MACO goes further and is explicitly metric-agnostic: a neural network outputs softmax probabilities and class representations are conditioned on the query. The evidence therefore distinguishes RCN's local, interpretable similarity learning from MACO's query-conditioned neural classifier, but neither excerpt supplies a common numeric table with the same backbone and episodes, so their accuracies cannot be ranked against each other or against fixed-distance prototypes from these snippets alone. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:0fa86bc29e24] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:8ddae53d33c7] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:2:c37dc575d3c8:claim:d5aad7ce0ffb] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:1:74ed040863a6:claim:3812293ab161]

Task-adaptive and contextual models broaden the experimental unit from one image pair to the whole episode. Meta-Metric-Learner combines a task-specific metric learner with a meta-learner that specifies the base model and evaluates standard episodes plus settings with flexible class counts in single-source and multi-source forms; this is a different stress test from the usual fixed 5-way protocol. QSFormer uses global query–support attention and local patch Transformers, while MSENet combines multi-stage embeddings, self-attention, and learned stage weights. These systems can improve representation and comparison jointly, which means an accuracy gain cannot be attributed solely to a better metric. Their results are comparable only to baselines re-run with matched backbones, attention modules, training data, and episode settings. [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:0b0752f4ac3d] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:d539e10e3cd6] [E:arxiv:2208.12398:abstract:claim:eb85178b6852] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:baa36cba9b0a]

Non-episodic and label-budget baselines are essential controls because apparent metric-learning gains may come from representation pretraining. The fine-tuning study reports that a network pretrained with standard cross-entropy and fine-tuned, especially transductively, outperforms then-current state-of-the-art methods on Mini-ImageNet, Tiered-ImageNet, CIFAR-FS, and FC-100 with the same hyper-parameters, and it also reports ImageNet-21k experiments. ProtoTransfer uses self-supervised prototype-style transfer and reports better performance than state-of-the-art unsupervised meta-learning methods on mini-ImageNet and comparable supervised-domain-shift performance with orders of magnitude fewer labels. These are not like-for-like comparisons with supervised inductive metric learners unless pretraining data, labels, and fine-tuning/transduction are matched; they do, however, show that a metric method must beat a strong embedding-and-fine-tuning baseline under the intended deployment regime. [E:arxiv:1909.02729:abstract:claim:5f189919bcf6] [E:arxiv:2006.11325:abstract:claim:d76dc15743ab]

Domain-specific benchmarks and unmatched results should remain separate from natural-image rankings. The FewSAR benchmark reimplements 15 classic methods in three categories under common SAR protocols and reports that, within that benchmark, metric-learning methods attain the best accuracy while meta-learning and fine-tuning methods perform poorly, with the authors attributing that pattern partly to biases of existing SAR datasets. The hyperspectral multi-level relation method adds class-level contrastive and set-level cross-attention relations and demonstrates gains over state-of-the-art methods in cross-domain few-shot hyperspectral classification. ABHFA-Net also reports disaster-image results, including up to 68.2% 1-shot and 78.3% 5-shot accuracy on AIDER. These findings support applicability in their respective sensor domains, but they are non-comparable with miniImageNet or CUB numbers and do not establish a universal ordering of metric-learning mechanisms. Limitations and Open Problems

Open problems and trade-offs. The first unresolved issue is that the three-stage decomposition—embedding, class representation, and comparator—does not imply that gains can be cleanly attributed to one stage. Many metric learners train an encoder, support-set aggregation, and nonlinear relation module end to end, while contextual Transformers or attention models can simultaneously alter image features and query–support interactions. As a result, an accuracy improvement over a simpler prototype baseline may come from a stronger backbone, additional parameters, task conditioning, or the comparison rule rather than from the metric idea alone. Future comparisons need controlled ablations that hold the encoder, training data, episode sampler, optimizer, augmentation, and inference mode fixed before claiming that a particular distance or class model is responsible. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2208.12398:abstract:claim:eb85178b6852] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:baa36cba9b0a]

A second problem is the fragility of class summaries estimated from one to five examples. Nearest-example comparisons avoid averaging but can be dominated by a noisy support image; a mean prototype is compact but assumes an approximately unimodal cluster and can erase pose, viewpoint, or part-level variation; distribution and subspace models express uncertainty or geometric span but still estimate those structures from very few samples. The reported robustness of subspace methods to noise and outliers is therefore conditional rather than a reason to discard prototypes. The practical implication is that no single support-set geometry is guaranteed to match every task: benchmark comparisons should include controlled support noise, outlier supports, multimodal classes, and varying shot counts rather than reporting only standard 1-shot and 5-shot means. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:32d2f0aedf14] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8969ee1e4e70]

Shot-count mismatch remains a concrete protocol problem. The Prototypical-Network analysis identifies the number of shots used during meta-training as a crucial hyperparameter and notes that performance is generally best when meta-training and meta-testing shot counts agree. This matters because many papers train on a fixed 5-way 1-shot or 5-shot objective and then present results for both settings, potentially conflating the quality of a class representation with favorable episode sampling. Methods should report performance when training shot count differs from deployment shot count, and ideally evaluate across a range of support-set sizes rather than treating 1-shot and 5-shot as isolated tasks. [E:arxiv:1909.11722:abstract:claim:ad5a8d7aede4]

Cross-domain generalization is not solved by in-domain episodic accuracy. The feature-wise-transformation paper motivates its method by observing that feature distributions differ across domains and that a metric function can overfit statistics seen during training; the deep K-tuplet and Proto-Triplet/ICNN papers respond mainly through embedding objectives and evaluate transfer from miniImageNet to datasets such as CUB, Dogs, Cars, and Caltech. These are complementary responses, but the evidence is tied to particular source–target pairs. A model that transfers to four natural-image datasets may still fail under sensor shift, remote-sensing imagery, disaster scenes, or hyperspectral data, so cross-domain claims should specify the source domain, target domains, label budget, and whether target data were used for tuning. [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:aafe927bcc74] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:2:ada74c4d4774:claim:83310823f8ec] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:abe1e207bc9c] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:2b40d78bb79f] [E:arxiv:2510.18326:abstract:claim:2c570434b933] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:430d78b68501]

The boundary between metric learning and strong representation learning is also still unsettled. A standard cross-entropy-pretrained network with careful fine-tuning, particularly transductive fine-tuning, is reported to outperform then-current few-shot systems on Mini-ImageNet, Tiered-ImageNet, CIFAR-FS, and FC-100 under the same hyper-parameters. ProtoTransfer further shows that self-supervised prototype-style transfer can be label-efficient and competitive under domain shift. These findings do not invalidate learned metrics, but they show that metric papers must separate the value of pretraining and target-label adaptation from the value of episodic similarity learning. Without such controls, leaderboard gains may overstate the contribution of the metric component. [E:arxiv:1909.02729:abstract:claim:5f189919bcf6] [E:arxiv:2006.11325:abstract:claim:d76dc15743ab]

Learned comparators introduce their own interpretability and identifiability trade-off. Fixed Euclidean or cosine distances are easy to inspect but may be too rigid across tasks; neural relation scores can model nonlinear, attribute-dependent matches, but a soft relation score need not satisfy metric axioms. MACO makes this explicit by replacing metric-space comparison with a query-conditioned neural classifier, and RCN addresses interpretability through region comparisons and activation maps. RCN-style visualizations are useful evidence about correspondence, but they do not by themselves prove that the highlighted regions causally determine the prediction. Comparator research therefore needs both metric-agnostic controls and explanation tests beyond visualization, such as perturbation or part-occlusion evaluations. [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:1:74ed040863a6:claim:3812293ab161] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:2:c37dc575d3c8:claim:d5aad7ce0ffb] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:0fa86bc29e24] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:8ddae53d33c7]

Task adaptation creates a flexibility–complexity trade-off. A task-invariant metric is simple and can handle different class counts, but the Meta-Metric-Learner paper argues that one metric is strained when tasks have flexible class numbers or come from less similar domains; task-specific metrics, query-conditioned representations, and attention over the full episode can adapt to those conditions. The cost is additional meta-learning machinery, greater dependence on the task distribution used during training, and more difficulty diagnosing whether adaptation improves semantic comparison or merely fits episode statistics. Adaptive methods should therefore be evaluated on held-out task structures, varying way counts, and domains not represented when the adaptation rule was learned, rather than only on fixed 5-way episodes. [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:0b0752f4ac3d] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:d539e10e3cd6] [E:arxiv:2208.12398:abstract:claim:eb85178b6852]

Benchmark heterogeneity continues to impede reliable ranking. The reviewed sources use MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, CIFAR-FS, FC-100, CUB, Caltech, Dogs, Cars, SAR, hyperspectral, and disaster datasets with different backbones, splits, supervision budgets, and application assumptions. FewSAR explicitly notes that SAR research has suffered from non-unified datasets and custom experimental setups, and it addresses this by providing common protocols and runtime analysis; domain-specific studies such as ABHFA-Net and the hyperspectral relation model report strong results in their own settings. Those numbers cannot be merged into a universal metric-learning leaderboard. The field needs common code, matched baselines, uncertainty estimates, runtime or parameter reporting, and separate leaderboards for in-domain, cross-domain natural-image, transductive, unsupervised, and sensor-specific tasks. [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:616f72ed5776] [E:arxiv:2510.18326:abstract:claim:2c570434b933] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:430d78b68501] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1]

Efficiency and deployment constraints are under-specified in much of the metric-learning evidence. Subspace construction, distribution estimation, multi-stage encoders, cross-attention, graph or Transformer relation modules, and task-specific metric adaptation may improve accuracy but add computation, memory, or tuning requirements. Conversely, a simple fixed-distance prototype can be inexpensive at inference but may underfit complex support structure. The FewSAR benchmark is distinctive in the selected sources because it analyzes both quantitative results and runtime under a common setting; most natural-image excerpts reviewed here do not provide enough matched latency, memory, parameter-count, or tuning-cost evidence. Accuracy alone therefore cannot determine which metric approach is preferable in a data-scarce, time-critical application. [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:616f72ed5776] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e] [E:arxiv:2208.12398:abstract:claim:eb85178b6852] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:baa36cba9b0a] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:0b0752f4ac3d]

Finally, scope discipline remains important. Few-shot metric learning is related to, but not identical to, optimization-based meta-learning, transfer learning, zero-shot recognition, and domain-specific classification. Zero-shot methods compare images with semantic attributes or class descriptions without labeled support examples, whereas few-shot metric methods compare against support examples or class models; natural-language adaptive-metric evidence may motivate task-adaptive image methods but does not establish image accuracy; and SAR or hyperspectral results demonstrate application fit rather than universal superiority. The most useful future work would preserve these distinctions while reporting matched ablations, cross-domain stress tests, label and compute budgets, and uncertainty, so that embedding, representation, and comparator contributions can be compared without turning method-specific evidence into an unsupported global ranking. Conclusion

The direct comparison favors a matched-component view rather than a single ranking: simple prototypes and fixed distances remain transparent baselines, while richer class models and learned comparators are justified only when matched evidence shows they address support noise, multimodality, local correspondence or task variation. Hybrid contextual models complicate attribution because they change features and comparison jointly. claim_records.text: The deep K-tuplet network extends the classical triplet network from deep metric learning for few-shot learning, utilizing the relationship among input samples to learn a general representation via episode-training.

The trained deep K-tuplet network can extract discriminative features for unseen novel categories and can be seamlessly incorporated with a non-linear distance metric function to facilitate few-shot classification.
The proposed method's result on the miniImageNet benchmark outperforms other metric-based few-shot classification methods.

When evaluated on Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs and Stanford Cars using the model trained with miniImageNet, the proposed method significantly outperforms prior methods, demonstrating superior capability to generalize to unseen classes.

The deep K-tuplet Network generalizes the triplet network to allow joint comparison with K negative samples in each mini-batch, making the feature embedding learning process more faithful to the few-shot classification problem with improved feature generalization.
The semi-hard mining sampling technique is an effective sampling strategy to sample informative hard triplets, which can speed up convergence and stabilize the training procedure.
The proposed method outperforms other metric-based methods and achieves competitive performance over other meta-based methods on the miniImageNet dataset.

The proposed method establishes a new experimental setting for evaluating the cross-domain generalization ability for few-shot classification algorithms, and its generalized results on CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, Stanford Cars and Caltech-101 excel other methods.

The proposed method performs target tasks based entirely on feed-forward without requiring further parameter updates, unlike meta-learning methods that need to fine-tune or update parameters for new unseen tasks.

claim_records.text: The proposed Proto-Triplet Loss is based on the original triplet loss with modifications needed to better work on few-shot scenarios.
The proposed ICNN loss is based on an inter and intra class nearest neighbors score, which helps assess the quality of embeddings obtained from the trained network.
The proposed loss functions achieve a significant improvement in accuracy in the miniImageNet benchmark compared to other metric-based few-shot learning methods by a margin of 2%.
The proposed methods demonstrate competitive generalization capabilities to other domains, including Caltech, CUB, Dogs and Cars datasets, compared with the state of the art.
The ICNN Loss measures the intra and inter class distances of batch points and assigns each data point an Inter and Intra Class Nearest Neighbors score.
The Proto-Triplet loss takes a query point as anchor, the prototype from the same class as positive point and the nearest prototype of different class as the negative point.
Using the proto-triplet loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 61.32% in the 5-way 1-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the proto-triplet loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 79.93% in the 5-way 5-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the ICNN Loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 60.79% in the 5-way 1-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the ICNN Loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 80.41% in the 5-way 5-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
The accuracy results of the proposed loss functions on Mini-Imagenet represent an improvement of about 2% compared to the state of the art.
The proposed methods are further tested on the CUB, Caltech, Stanford Dogs and Stanford Cars datasets to assess generalization capabilities, obtaining satisfactory results.

claim_records.text: The proposed Metric-Agnostic Conditional network (MACO) architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Caltech-UCSD birds fine-grained classification task.

The MACO architecture replaces the metric space comparison used in traditional metric-learning few-shot approaches with a learned neural network architecture, outputting a softmax probability distribution rather than a true distance or similarity metric.
The MACO network achieves its best performance only when it is allowed to condition each class representation based on the target (query) image.
The MACO network consists of four distinct stages trained fully end-to-end: a feature stage, a relational stage, a conditioning stage, and a classifier stage.

The MACO feature stage uses a convolutional architecture identical to that of Ravi & Larochelle (2017), composed of four convolutional blocks each with a 3×3 kernel, 32 filters, batch normalization, ELU activation, and 2×2 max pooling, followed by a linear layer producing an 800-dimensional image representation vector.

The MACO relational stage uses a relational network to perform pairwise comparisons of images within each support set class, producing a single order-insensitive vector representation for the class, with parameters shared across all classes.
Traditional metric-learning few-shot approaches place new categories within a learned metric space, most often using a pre-defined distance metric such as Euclidean or cosine distance.

claim_records.text: The proposed Meta-Metric-Learner hybrid model combines optimization-based and metric-based meta-learning approaches, consisting of a task-specific metric-based learner as a base model and a meta-learner that learns and specifies the base model.
The Meta-Metric-Learner model is able to handle flexible numbers of classes as well as generate more generalized metrics for classification across tasks.

Experiments show the Meta-Metric-Learner approach obtains superior performance in both the standard k-shot N-way few-shot learning setting and a new realistic few-shot setting with flexible class numbers in both single-source and multi-source forms.

Existing optimization-based meta-learning approaches require task-specific classifiers to be homogeneous-structured to ease parameter prediction, and thus can only handle few-shot learning problems where tasks share a uniform number of classes.
Existing metric-based meta-learning approaches learn one task-invariant metric for all tasks, and require tasks to come from a similar domain such that a uniform metric works across tasks.

In the Meta-Metric-Learner, the meta learner operating across tasks uses an optimization-based meta-model to discover good parameters and gradient descent in task-specific base learners, while the base learner exploits a metric-based model and parameterizes task metrics using weight prediction from the optimization-based meta-learner.

The Meta-Metric-Learner is able to handle unbalanced classes in meta-train and meta-test sets, and generates task-specific metrics leveraging weight prediction from the meta-learner given task instances.

Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) explicitly trains initial parameters of a CNN model such that a small number of gradient update steps with a small amount of training data from a new task will produce good generalization performance on that task.

claim_records.text: The Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot (UAFS) framework models uncertainty of query-prototype similarity and performs uncertainty-aware optimization for image classification.

Rather than using a scalar, the similarity between a query feature zi and a prototype feature cj is modeled by a distribution (probabilistic similarity) based on graph-based similarity uncertainty estimation.
For a query sample xi and N prototypes in the support set, each query-prototype pair is treated as a node and a graph-based model jointly infers the similarity uncertainty σi,j for each pair.

fact_fields.method: Graph-based model for joint similarity uncertainty inference

claim_records.text: The network is optimized with similarity-based classification losses that exploit the estimated similarity uncertainty.
The proposed Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot framework converts observed similarities to probabilistic representations and incorporates them into the loss for more effective optimization.
A graph-based model is utilized to estimate the uncertainty of query-support pair similarities in the proposed framework.
Extensive experiments show the proposed method brings significant improvements on top of a strong baseline and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

In few-shot image classification, the set of category-specific prototypes (averaged support sample feature embeddings) acts as a similarity-based classifier to identify a query sample's category by finding the nearest prototype in the embedding space.
During training, a query sample's logit vector (classification probability) is obtained by feeding similarities between the query sample and prototypes to a SoftMax function.

For each query-prototype pair, the observed feature similarity between the query and prototype is converted from a deterministic scalar to a distribution, with the distribution's variance characterizing the uncertainty of the observed similarity.
Aleatoric uncertainty identifies the confidence level of the network on its output for a sample, capturing noise inherent in the observations.

For few-shot image classification, the network has different uncertainties on calculated similarities of different query-prototype pairs, and higher uncertainty corresponds to less reliable estimated similarity.

claim_records.text: Region Comparison Network (RCN) is a metric learning based method proposed for interpretable few-shot image classification, designed to reveal how few-shot learning works in a neural network and identify mutually related regions between query and support set images.
Region Activation Mapping (RAM) is a visualization strategy designed to intuitively explain what RCN has learned by visualizing intermediate variables in the network.
The interpretability of RCN can be generalized from the task level to the category level, which corresponds to identifying prototypical parts that support the final classification decision of RCN.
Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that RCN outperforms existing baselines for few-shot image classification.

RCN's final prediction module learns a generated weight of regions to explain which regions in a support sample are similar to locations in a query sample and which regions the model prefers to compare.
RCN is designed to generate a region weight in the final stage to define which common parts between support and query samples most influence the final similarity score.
Existing few-shot learning works are grouped into metric-based models (e.g., matching networks, prototypical networks) and gradient-based models (e.g., MAML, MetaSGD).

claim_records.text: MF-Adapter is a proposed method that combines complementary strengths of low-level local representations (LRs) and high-level semantic representations for CLIP-based few-shot image classification.
Meta-Feature Unit (MF-Unit) is a simple yet effective local similarity metric designed to measure category-consistent local context in an inductive manner.
MF-Adapter is trained to map image features to MF-Unit to generalize intra-class knowledge between unseen images and the support set.
Extensive experiments show MF-Adapter outperforms state-of-the-art CLIP downstream few-shot classification methods, including on challenging visual classification tasks.

MF-Unit is obtained by inductive representation of local feature maps on different scales using sliding windows with different perceptual fields, containing rich local information representing category-consistent characteristics.
MF-Unit is calculated via inductive max and mean operations on each sliding window to compress parameters and reduce redundancy, representing category-consistent features with inductive knowledge.

During inference, MF-Adapter first infers test images into MF-Units at different levels and scales, retrieves few-shot knowledge in the MF-Unit space of the support set to get local logits, then combines this with the original CLIP high-level prediction for the final prediction.
MF-Adapter achieves state-of-the-art performance across 11 widely adopted datasets for few-shot classification, and is the first work to utilize the local similarity of CLIP in few-shot learning.

In few-shot classification scenarios with insufficient seen images, the standard pre-training and fine-tuning paradigm for CLIP does not produce improved results, so common practice is to fix CLIP pre-training weights and learn a lightweight adaptation module.
Tip-Adapter achieves large performance improvements over both prompt-based methods and CLIP-Adapter on several classification datasets by fine-tuning a trainable query-key cache layer on top of CLIP.

claim_records.text: The proposed subspace representation learning (SRL) framework represents an image using a subspace in local CNN feature space and measures similarity between two images via a weighted subspace distance (WSD).
When K images are available per class, the SRL framework develops two types of template subspaces to aggregate K-shot information: the prototypical subspace (PS) and the discriminative subspace (DS).
The SRL framework extends metric learning based techniques from vector to subspace representation.
Using subspace representation instead of the previously adopted global vector representation can effectively preserve the spatial structure and diversity within an image.

fact_fields.method: subspace representation vs global vector representation

claim_records.text: Experimental results on three public benchmark datasets (MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB)) demonstrate competitive or superior performance of the SRL method compared to previous state-of-the-art approaches.

claim_records.text: Metric-based few-shot image classification directly measures relations between query images and support classes to learn transferable feature embeddings.
Previous work using image-level feature representations cannot effectively estimate a class's distribution due to the scarcity of samples.
Local descriptor based representations can achieve richer representations than image-level based representations.

Existing local descriptor based few-shot learning works still rely on a less effective instance-level metric, especially a symmetric metric, to measure relations between query images and support classes.
An asymmetric measure is argued to be more suitable for metric-based few-shot learning given the natural asymmetric relation between a query image and a support class.

fact_fields.method: asymmetric measure for metric-based few-shot learning

claim_records.text: The proposed Asymmetric Distribution Measure (ADM) network calculates a joint local and global asymmetric measure between two multivariate local distributions of queries and classes for few-shot learning.
A task-aware Contrastive Measure Strategy (CMS) is proposed to further enhance the measure function in the ADM network.
On miniImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 3.02% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.
On tieredImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 1.56% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.

claim_records.text: RankDNN casts relevance ranking for image retrieval as binary ranking relation classification.
Ranking relation classification is sample efficient and domain agnostic in comparison to image classification.
The core component of RankDNN is a simple MLP that takes as input an image triplet encoded as the difference between two vector-Kronecker products, and outputs a binary relevance ranking order.
RankMLP can be built on top of any state-of-the-art feature extractors.
RankDNN can be flexibly fused with other post-processing methods.
During meta test, RankDNN ranks support images according to their similarity with the query samples, and each query sample is assigned the class label of its nearest neighbor.
RankDNN can effectively improve the performance of its baselines based on a variety of backbones.
RankDNN outperforms previous state-of-the-art algorithms on multiple few-shot learning benchmarks including miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, Caltech-UCSD Birds, and CIFAR-FS.
Experiments on the cross-domain challenge demonstrate the superior transferability of RankDNN.

claim_records.text: The proposed QSFormer model integrates a global query-support sample Transformer (sampleFormer) branch and a local patch Transformer (patchFormer) learning branch to simultaneously address the two core challenges of few-shot classification.

The sampleFormer branch of QSFormer adopts Encoder, Decoder and Cross-Attention to respectively model Support representation, Query image representation, and metric learning for few-shot classification.

The local patch Transformer (patchFormer) branch of QSFormer extracts structural representation for each image sample by capturing the long-range dependence of local image patches, serving as a complement to the global learning branch.
A novel Cross-scale Interactive Feature Extractor (CIFE) is proposed to extract and fuse multi-scale CNN features as an effective backbone module for the QSFormer few-shot learning method.
All modules of QSFormer are integrated into a unified framework and trained in an end-to-end manner.
Extensive experiments on four popular datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed QSFormer for few-shot classification.

claim_records.text: Traditional metric-based few-shot classification methods typically rely on a single distance value between the query feature and support feature, overlooking the contribution of shallow features.

The proposed method uses a multi-output embedding network that maps samples into distinct feature spaces by extracting feature vectors at different stages, enabling the model to capture both global and abstract features.
Employing a self-attention mechanism improves the refinement of features at each stage, leading to more robust representations and improved overall performance.
Assigning learnable weights to each stage of the multi-output embedding network significantly improved performance and results.
Comprehensive evaluations of the proposed method were conducted on the MiniImageNet and FC100 datasets in the 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot scenarios.
Cross-domain tasks across eight benchmark datasets were performed for the proposed method, achieving high accuracy in the testing domains.
The evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in comparison to state-of-the-art approaches.
The goal of few-shot classification is to train a classifier using a limited number of samples while maintaining satisfactory performance.

The proposed multi-level correlation network (MLCN) for few-shot image classification effectively captures local information by using a multi-level descriptor of an image.
The self-correlation module and cross-correlation module in MLCN learn the semantic correspondence relation of local information based on learned representations.
The pattern-correlation module in MLCN captures the pattern of fine-grained images and finds relevant structural patterns between base classes and novel classes.
Extensive experiments and analysis show the effectiveness of the proposed MLCN method on four widely-used few-shot image classification benchmarks.

claim_records.text: ProtoTransfer is a self-supervised transfer learning approach that constructs a metric embedding clustering unlabeled prototypical samples and their augmentations closely together, with the pre-trained embedding serving as a starting point for few-shot classification via class cluster summarization and fine-tuning.
ProtoTransfer outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised meta-learning methods on few-shot tasks from the mini-ImageNet dataset.
In few-shot experiments with realistic domain shift, ProtoTransfer achieves comparable performance to supervised methods while requiring orders of magnitude fewer labels.
Common transfer learning has been shown to outperform supervised meta-learning in settings with realistic domain shift.
Unsupervised meta-learning methods exchange the annotation requirement for a reduction in few-shot classification performance.

claim_records.text: HyperShot is a proposed few-shot learning model that fuses kernels and the hypernetwork paradigm.
Unlike reference approaches that apply a gradient-based adjustment of parameters, HyperShot switches classification module parameters depending on the task's embedding.
HyperShot utilizes a hypernetwork that takes aggregated information from support data and returns classifier parameters handcrafted for the considered problem.
HyperShot introduces a kernel-based representation of support examples delivered to the hypernetwork to create the parameters of the classification module.
HyperShot relies on relations between embeddings of support examples instead of direct feature values provided by backbone models.
The HyperShot approach enables the model to adapt to highly different tasks.

claim_records.text: Two identified crucial advantages of contrastive learning compared to meta learning are comprehensive utilization of graph nodes and the power of graph augmentations.
COLA is a proposed paradigm for few-shot node classification that integrates the strengths of contrastive learning and meta learning.
COLA employs graph augmentations to identify semantically similar nodes, enabling construction of meta-tasks without the need for label information.
COLA can utilize all nodes to construct meta-tasks, further reducing the risk of overfitting.
Extensive experiments validate the essentiality of each component in COLA's design.
COLA achieves new state-of-the-art on all few-shot node classification tasks tested.
There is limited understanding of the reasons why graph contrastive learning combined with fine-tuning outperforms meta learning methods on few-shot node classification.

claim_records.text: The proposed Siamese Transformer Network (STN) employs two parallel branch networks utilizing the pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture to extract global and local features respectively.
The STN implementation uses the ViT-Small network architecture, with branch networks initialized with pre-trained model parameters obtained through self-supervised learning.
The STN applies Euclidean distance measure to global features and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measure to local features.
The STN integrates the two feature metrics by first applying L2 normalization then weighting the normalized results to obtain the final similarity score.
During the training phase, the STN adopts a meta-learning approach to fine-tune the entire network.

Extensive experiments show the STN framework achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines on four popular few-shot classification benchmarks in both 5-shot and 1-shot scenarios.

claims: The presented spatial-relational few-shot image classification architecture has an ultra-lightweight parameter count ranging from 22,249 to 34,917.

Under the strictly matched iso-episode-budget protocol (250 meta-training episodes, 5 canonical seeds, 600 evaluation episodes per seed), the architecture achieves consistent 5-shot accuracy gains across all five seeds over Prototypical Networks, Relation Networks, and MAML on both CIFAR-FS and MiniImageNet.
The architecture uses 27-53% fewer parameters than any of the compared baselines (Prototypical Networks, Relation Networks, MAML).
The architecture converges in fewer training episodes than the compared baselines.
The architecture generalizes better to the unseen fine-grained CUB-200-2011 birds domain with zero retraining than the compared baselines.
The architecture is more robust to 50% occlusion than all three compared baselines.
The architecture is more robust to 25% spatial translation than all three compared baselines.

Falsification ablations (zeroing relational tokens at inference and retraining without them entirely) show the architecture's pairwise relational computation is not the primary driver of its performance; the content-adaptive patch locator is.
A capacity sweep shows a genuine accuracy plateau near 22-35k parameters for the architecture.

claim_records.text: The proposed Mutual Centralized Learning (MCL) method affiliates two disjoint sets of dense features in a bidirectional paradigm, associating each local feature with a particle that can bidirectionally random walk in a discrete feature space by the affiliations.
MCL estimates class probability via features' accessibility, which measures the expected number of visits to the support features of that class in a Markov process.
MCL relates to learning a centrality on an affiliation network and can be plugged into existing methods by highlighting centralized local features.
Experiments show that the MCL method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both miniImageNet and tieredImageNet.

claim_records.text: The proposed Generative Dual Adversarial Network provides a unified framework for visual->semantic mapping, semantic->visual mapping, and metric learning for generalized zero-shot learning.

The proposed model consists of a feature generator that generates visual features from class embeddings, a regressor that maps visual features back to class embeddings, and a discriminator that evaluates closeness between image features and class embeddings.
All three components of the proposed model are trained under the combination of cyclic consistency loss and dual adversarial loss.
Experimental results show the proposed model preserves higher accuracy in classifying images from seen classes compared to prior approaches.
Experimental results show the proposed model performs better than existing state-of-the-art models in classifying images from unseen classes.

claim_records.text: The proposed patch-driven relational refinement learns cache adapter weights from intra-image patch dependencies rather than treating an image embedding as a monolithic vector.

The introduced relational gated graph attention network constructs a patch graph and performs edge-aware attention to emphasize informative inter-patch interactions, producing context-enriched patch embeddings.
A learnable multi-aggregation pooling composes context-enriched patch embeddings into compact, task-discriminative representations that better align cache keys with the target few-shot classes.
The proposed graph refinement is used only during training to distil relational structure into the cache, incurring no additional inference cost beyond standard cache lookup.
Final predictions are obtained by a residual fusion of cache similarity scores with CLIP zero-shot logits.

claim_records.text: Few-shot Cosine Transformer (FS-CT) consists of a learnable prototypical embedding network to obtain categorical representations from support samples with hard cases, and a transformer encoder to effectively achieve the relational map from two different support and query samples.

Cosine Attention, a more robust and stable attention module, enhances the transformer module significantly and improves FS-CT performance from 5% to over 20% in accuracy compared to the default scaled dot-product mechanism.
FS-CT performs competitive results in mini-ImageNet, CUB-200, and CIFAR-FS on 1-shot learning and 5-shot learning tasks across backbones and few-shot configurations.
A custom few-shot dataset for Yoga pose recognition was developed to demonstrate the potential of the FS-CT algorithm for practical application.
FS-CT with cosine attention is a lightweight, simple few-shot algorithm applicable for a wide range of applications such as healthcare, medical, and security surveillance.

claim_records.text: HelixFormer is a Transformer-based double-helix model proposed to achieve cross-image object semantic relation mining in a bidirectional and symmetrical manner for few-shot fine-grained image classification.
HelixFormer consists of two steps: Relation Mining Process (RMP) across different branches, and Representation Enhancement Process (REP) within each individual branch.

The designed RMP in HelixFormer enables each branch to extract fine-grained object-level Cross-image Semantic Relation Maps (CSRMs) using information from the other branch, ensuring better cross-image interaction in semantically related local object regions.

With the aid of CSRMs, the developed REP in HelixFormer strengthens extracted features for discovered semantically-related local regions in each branch, boosting the model's ability to distinguish subtle feature differences of fine-grained objects.

Extensive experiments on five public fine-grained benchmarks demonstrate that HelixFormer achieves much better performance over most state-of-the-art methods under 1-shot and 5-shot few-shot scenarios.
The code for HelixFormer is publicly available at https://github.com/JiakangYuan/HelixFormer.

claim_records.text: In few-shot learning, the conventional pooled global feature is likely to lose useful local characteristics.

Existing deep descriptor-based FSL methods generally take all deep descriptors from neural networks into consideration, ignoring that some descriptors are useless in classification due to their limited receptive field.

The paper argues that a Mutual Nearest Neighbor (MNN) relation should be established to explicitly select query descriptors most relevant to each task and discard less relevant ones from aggregative clutters in FSL.
The proposed method for FSL is Discriminative Mutual Nearest Neighbor Neural Network (DMN4).

claim_records.text: Extensive experiments demonstrate that DMN4 outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on both fine-grained and generalized datasets.

claim_records.text: FiT combines fixed pretrained backbones, fine-tuned FiLM adapter layers, automatically configured Naive Bayes classifiers, and episodic training to produce parameter efficient image classification models with superior low-shot classification accuracy.
FiT achieves better classification accuracy than the leading Big Transfer (BiT) algorithm at low-shot across a wide range of downstream datasets.
FiT achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on the challenging VTAB-1k benchmark using fewer than 1% of the updateable parameters.

FiT demonstrates parameter efficiency and superior accuracy in distributed low-shot applications including model personalization and federated learning where model update size is an important performance metric.
The parameter efficiency of FiT enables few-shot learning, inexpensive model updates for personalization, and communication efficient federated learning.

claim_records.text: Most current few shot methods train an encoder on a base dataset rich in labeled examples to obtain representations of support instances for novel classes, but test instances from a distribution different to the base distribution have poor feature representation quality that degrades performance.

BaseTransformers attends to the most relevant regions of the base dataset feature space and improves support instance representations by using well-trained feature representations of base dataset points closest to each support instance during meta-test time.
Experiments on three benchmark datasets show that BaseTransformers works well for several backbones and achieves state-of-the-art results in the inductive one shot setting.

claim_records.text: Prototypical Random Walk Networks (PRWN) is a semi-supervised few-shot learning approach built on top of Prototypical Networks (PN).
The developed random walk semi-supervised loss enables the network to learn representations that are compact and well-separated.

Compact and well-separated class representations can be achieved by modeling the prototypical random walk notion without needing additional graph-NN parameters or requiring a transductive setting where a collective test set is provided.
The PRWN model outperforms baselines in most benchmarks, with significant improvements in some cases.

PRWN trained with 40% of the data as labeled achieves 50.89% accuracy in the 1-shot mini-Imagenet case, outperforming fully supervised Prototypical Networks trained on 100% of the labels which achieves 49.4% accuracy.

# Metric Learning for Few-Shot Image Classification: An Embedding–Representation–Metric Comparison

## Abstract

Metric-learning few-shot classifiers are best compared by where their main bias acts: the encoder, the support-set class model, or the comparison rule. Embedding losses and modulation target transferable features; nearest examples, prototypes, distributions and subspaces encode support information differently; fixed, learned, query-conditioned and task-adaptive comparators vary decision flexibility. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:0fa86bc29e24] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:0b0752f4ac3d] [E:arxiv:2006.11325:abstract:claim:d76dc15743ab] Reported gains do not support one universal winner. K-tuplet and Proto-Triplet/ICNN show embedding and cross-dataset benefits, distribution and subspace methods address uncertainty or geometry, and RCN or MACO add learned relational comparison, but results differ in backbone, shots, datasets, pretraining, inference and label budget. In-domain, cross-domain, sensor-domain and label-efficient transfer settings must therefore be compared separately. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:abe1e207bc9c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:53d7fbe2de7c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:22bea6df5855] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:307bf74255b7] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:2b40d78bb79f] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:0ec5dc39dacf] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:32d2f0aedf14] [E:arxiv:2510.18326:abstract:claim:2c570434b933] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8969ee1e4e70] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:efa61445b15c] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:0fa86bc29e24] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:8ddae53d33c7] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:2:c37dc575d3c8:claim:d5aad7ce0ffb] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:1:74ed040863a6:claim:3812293ab161] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:aafe927bcc74] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:2:ada74c4d4774:claim:83310823f8ec] [E:arxiv:1909.02729:abstract:claim:5f189919bcf6] [E:arxiv:2006.11325:abstract:claim:d76dc15743ab] [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:616f72ed5776] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:430d78b68501] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:3e17d5d5f5a5]

## Introduction

Few-shot image classification asks a model to assign query images to classes when each novel class supplies only a small labeled support set, commonly one to five examples. The central difficulty is that ordinary supervised training can overfit to these few labels; metric-learning approaches respond by learning an embedding space and/or a similarity function in which same-class samples are close and different-class samples are far apart, then classifying a query by its relation to support samples or aggregated class representations. This review therefore compares approaches by the stage at which their main inductive bias operates: the image embedding, the class representation, and the distance or comparison rule. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:0fa86bc29e24] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1]

The standard episode makes the comparison structure explicit: a support set contains the few labeled images for the task's classes, and a query set contains unlabeled images from those classes. A feature encoder maps both sets into an embedding space, after which a metric function compares query features with support examples or class models to produce predictions. This framing covers nearest-example methods, prototype methods, distribution or subspace models, and learned relation networks, while excluding methods whose main mechanism is gradient-based task adaptation rather than comparison in a learned space. [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:aafe927bcc74] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:efa61445b15c]

The organizing choice used here is the review's three-stage grouping—learning feature embeddings, learning class representations, and learning distance measures—rather than a universal taxonomy. These dimensions are complementary: one method may improve the encoder, another may replace a mean prototype with a distribution or subspace, and a third may replace a fixed Euclidean or cosine comparison with a learned relation model. Metric learning can also be trained episodically as meta-learning, so the labels “metric-based” and “meta-learning” are not mutually exclusive. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb]

The comparison must also distinguish in-domain from cross-domain evaluation. In the familiar mini-ImageNet-style protocol, base and novel classes are drawn from the same benchmark domain; in cross-domain few-shot learning, the model is trained on one source domain, such as mini-ImageNet, and tested on novel classes from datasets such as CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, Stanford Cars, or Caltech-101. Consequently, accuracy under same-domain episodes does not by itself establish robustness to domain shift, and later sections keep datasets, shots, backbones, baselines, and training settings together before drawing any comparative conclusion. [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:aafe927bcc74] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:53d7fbe2de7c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:22bea6df5855]

## Background and Method Taxonomy

Taxonomy used in this review. The methods are organized by the three metric-learning stages identified in the reviewed survey: learning feature embeddings, learning class representations, and learning distance or similarity measures. This is an analytical grouping for comparing mechanisms, not a claim that every paper uses these labels or that a model belongs to only one stage. A single architecture can contribute at several stages—for example, an episodic encoder, an aggregated prototype, and a learned relation module can be trained end to end. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:3f2cc983fda1] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d6b4cf8f5deb]

Embedding-centered approaches place most of the model's adaptation burden on the feature map. Their premise is that a discriminative, task-general embedding should pull same-class images together and push different-class images apart before the final comparison. Examples in the sources include Siamese-style and triplet-like embedding learning, deep K-tuplet learning with multiple negatives, task-specific feature transformers or modulation, self-attention or multi-stage embeddings, and query–support Transformers that refine representations using context from the whole episode. These methods still need a decision rule, but their main novelty is what counts as a comparable feature and whether features are task-agnostic or task-conditioned. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_few_shot_deep_metric_learning_methods:0:c53378070ee7:claim:f4690eeeb5d0] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:abe1e207bc9c] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:2:ada74c4d4774:claim:83310823f8ec] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:baa36cba9b0a] [E:arxiv:2208.12398:abstract:claim:eb85178b6852]

Class-representation approaches differ in how the few support examples summarize a class. Early nearest-example methods compare a query directly with individual support embeddings. Point-prototype methods replace that set of comparisons with a reference vector, typically a simple or weighted mean of support features. Distributional and subspace approaches instead model uncertainty or geometric structure: variational representations estimate class distributions and can use KL divergence, Deep Subspace Network represents each class by a low-dimensional subspace and assigns a query by nearest projected distance, while SRL represents images or class templates as subspaces in local CNN feature space. The relevant distinction is therefore not merely “prototype versus non-prototype,” but whether a class is encoded as isolated points, one vector, a distribution, or a subspace. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:1f184b2f7f51] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:32d2f0aedf14] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8969ee1e4e70]

Distance-centered approaches vary the comparison rule after features and class summaries are formed. Fixed-rule methods use a predefined relation such as Euclidean or cosine distance. Learned-similarity methods train a network to score query–support or query–prototype pairs; Relation Network and Region Comparison Network fall in this broad family, with RCN additionally designed to expose corresponding image regions through its comparison and visualization mechanism. A further distinction is that a learned comparator producing class scores is not necessarily a mathematical metric: MACO explicitly replaces metric-space comparison with a neural classifier and conditions class representations on the query, so its authors describe it as metric-agnostic rather than a true metric-learning method. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:efa61445b15c] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:0fa86bc29e24] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:abstract:claim:8ddae53d33c7] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:2:c37dc575d3c8:claim:d5aad7ce0ffb] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:1:74ed040863a6:claim:3812293ab161]

Task conditioning supplies another useful comparison axis. A task-invariant metric assumes one embedding and comparison rule can transfer across episodes from a similar domain, whereas task-specific methods adapt features, metrics, or class representations to the current support set. The Meta-Metric-Learner paper motivates this split by arguing that a single task-invariant metric is strained when tasks contain varying class counts or come from less similar domains; it combines a task-specific metric learner with a meta-learner that specifies the base model. Likewise, cross-domain feature-wise modulation targets distribution shift by perturbing encoder activations during training so the downstream metric is less tied to seen-domain feature statistics. These axes cut across the three-stage taxonomy: conditioning may be implemented in the encoder, class model, comparator, or a hybrid meta-model. [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:0b0752f4ac3d] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:d539e10e3cd6] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:2:ada74c4d4774:claim:83310823f8ec] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:aafe927bcc74]

Boundaries and adjacent objectives. Metric-based few-shot classification should be distinguished from optimization-based meta-learning, whose central mechanism is learning an initialization or update rule for task-specific parameters, and from ordinary transfer learning or fine-tuning, where a source-pretrained classifier is adapted to target labels. These paradigms can overlap: metric embeddings may be learned through episodic meta-training, and self-supervised or transfer-trained embeddings may later be used with prototypes. The taxonomy also should not be confused with zero-shot recognition, which compares images to semantic class descriptions or attributes rather than to a few labeled support images, or with domain-specific applications such as SAR and hyperspectral classification, where metric learning is a method rather than a separate task definition. Efficiency, interpretability, and cross-domain robustness are evaluation objectives or design constraints; they do not by themselves define a separate metric-learning family.
